platform-vs-devops-boundary.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'built a platform' because you shipped a portal. A portal with incomplete templates, environments, secrets, or support paths is a boundary teams route around. The deliverable is a paved path teams choose because it is easier than the alternative — not a wall they climb over.

platform-vs-devops-boundary.text: A product team needs to launch a new service by Friday. There is no template, ownership of the deploy is a shrug, and the steps live in one engineer's terminal history. The platform lead says 'just use the portal' — and the team quietly ships a hand-built pipeline instead, because the portal stops at 'create repo' and leaves them alone with secrets, environments, and on-call.

Platform engineering treats the platform as a product and the developer as the customer. The whole game is a boundary decision: which delivery work becomes a paved golden path the platform owns, and which stays with the team — drawn so teams adopt it instead of bypassing it.

platform-vs-devops-boundary.reveal: A portal is a doorway, not a path. The failure this lesson exists to kill: the platform creates a portal but teams bypass it because templates, environments, secrets, and support paths are incomplete. A boundary is only real if the paved path is end-to-end — repo AND CI/CD AND environment creation AND secrets AND observability AND a support path — and lower-friction than hand-rolling. 'We have a portal' quietly assumes adoption it hasn't earned.

storyboard.say: A product team needs a new service live by Friday, so they walk up to the Developer Portal as their single entry point.
On the paved golden path, the portal generates a Service Template — no hand-written scaffolding, no copied boilerplate.
That template wires up CI/CD and infrastructure-as-code automatically, so delivery pipeline and infra come pre-built.
CI/CD then provisions secrets and observability, closing the loop on the whole platform-owned lane.
The finished service hands off to a Support Path the platform owns — ownership stays clear, not a shrug.
But if any segment is missing, the team leaves the portal and builds the pipeline by hand to hit the deadline.
That hand-built pipeline produces ownership drift — steps trapped in one terminal history, nobody accountable.
The lesson: the golden path only wins if it's complete — pave every segment or teams quietly bypass and drift.

developer-journey-mapping.text: The platform team ships a shiny Backstage portal, demos it to leadership, and celebrates. Six weeks later half the teams still deploy with hand-rolled YAML and a Slack thread — because the golden path stopped at "create service" and left secrets, environments, and support as an exercise for the reader.

An internal platform is a product, and its users are developers launching services under a clock. Developer journey mapping is the first move of the platform product model: trace the real path from intent to running service and mark every step where cognitive load spikes — because that spike is exactly where teams route around you.

developer-journey-mapping.prompt: Your portal has a beautiful "Create Service" button and adoption is still low. Before you add more features — what is most likely wrong? Answer before reading on.
developer-journey-mapping.reveal: The journey has a cliff, not a missing feature. "Create Service" is step one of a journey that also needs a template that compiles, a CI/CD run that goes green, an environment that provisions, secrets that are wired, observability that appears, and a support path when it breaks. Teams bypass the platform at the FIRST step where they hit a wall and no paved road continues — usually secrets or environment creation. More buttons on step one do not fix a cliff on step four. You have to map where the road ends and pave past it.

developer-journey-mapping.intro: The golden-path service template — and proving it with a dry run. Trace the complete platform artifact before implementing its deterministic evidence model.
steps: Start from the developer's inputs: name, owner, tier — the three things a team knows on day 0. The golden path asks for nothing they cannot answer without a meeting.
Template + CI/CD: the pavement that already works: These are the accent stages on the map. A rendered Deployment and a workflow that goes green on first push — the win teams already get today.

Environment + secrets: the friction cliff, now paved: This is the warning node — the step where the old journey ended. external-secrets binds Vault at deploy so secrets are never hand-copied into git. This one line is why teams stop bypassing.
Observability + support: complete the journey: Auto-attached OpenTelemetry and a generated runbook + on-call route. The journey does not end at "deployed" — it ends at "the developer can operate it."

Prove it with inspection hooks: --dry-run=server validates against the live API without applying; terraform plan shows the env with 0 destroys; helm template proves no undefined values. Proof the path works BEFORE a team trusts it.

# The golden-path service template — and proving it with a dry run
#
# Mission: Take a real (or realistic) service-launch the platform must support and produce platform_golden_path_review_packet.md: the developer journey mapped end-to-end (day-0 provision → deploy → observe → get help), the friction step where teams bypass the platform, the selected golden path, the rejected option, a verification hook output, and one reviewer objection answered.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Read your journey aloud from the developer's seat: intent → provision → deploy → observe → get-help. If any stage is a platform feature ("we have a catalog") instead of a developer action ("the team waits 2 days for a namespace"), rewrite it from their side.
# 2. Point to the exact step where a team would bypass the platform today. If you cannot name one, you mapped the brochure — find the cliff.
# 3. Run at least one inspection hook (kubectl apply --dry-run=server, terraform plan, or helm template) against your golden-path output and attach the result. A described path is not a proven path.
# 4. Confirm secrets and environment are on the paved road, not in "see docs" — this is the most common place the journey silently ends.
# 5. Check that the golden path lowers cognitive load WITHOUT hiding ownership or blast radius. Name what the developer still owns after adopting it.
# 6. State the invalidation condition: what result would make you say this golden path fails? (e.g., the template renders but terraform plan wants to destroy a shared resource.)
#
# Work only in the TODO function. Run every fixture and compare every output line.
# Local execution is practice feedback; it does not create controlled mastery evidence.

STAGES = [
    # (stage, wait_hours, manual_steps, docs_only)
    ("intent: request a new service", 0,  1, False),
    ("provision: repo + namespace",   48, 2, False),
    ("deploy: first green pipeline",  2,  3, False),
    ("secrets: bind vault path",      0,  6, True),
    ("observe: dashboards + traces",  4,  2, False),
    ("get-help: who do I ask",        24, 1, True),
]

def friction(wait_hours, manual_steps, docs_only):
    # waiting hurts, hand-work hurts double, a docs-only stage means the
    # pavement ends and the developer is alone: heavy penalty.
    return wait_hours + 2 * manual_steps + (40 if docs_only else 0)

storyboard.say: Start from the developer's seat: a real intent, launching a service under a clock. This is where the journey begins.

The portal has 100% coverage on the slide and 0% adoption in the deploy logs.

Platform-as-a-product means the golden path is your product, and adoption is your only real metric. This lesson turns 'we built a portal' into 'we defined the smallest paved road a team can walk from empty repo to a running, observed, owned service' — the artifact you carry into the platform capstone.

Cognitive load doesn't disappear; it just moves to the team, who then route around you. A golden path is measured at the LAST mile it covers, not the first.

golden-path-definition.code:
# Golden Path: HTTP Service (paved road v1)
## Context
- Journey: empty repo -> first request served + owned + observed, target < 30 min
- Constraint (non-negotiable): NO team hand-writes Kubernetes YAML or Terraform

## Template contract (what `backstage scaffold http-service` guarantees)
- [x] Repo + Dockerfile + Helm chart (helm template renders clean)
- [x] CI/CD: build -> test -> deploy, no per-team pipeline authoring
- [x] Env: Terraform-provisioned namespace + ingress (terraform plan)
- [x] Secrets: Vault path auto-bound to the namespace (NOT left to team)
- [x] Observability: OpenTelemetry SDK + default SLO dashboard on day one
- [x] Support: CODEOWNERS + on-call rotation named at scaffold time

## Inspection proofs (attach outputs)
$ helm template ./chart | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -
  service/orders configured (dry run)
  deployment.apps/orders configured (dry run)
$ terraform plan
  Plan: 3 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy   # namespace, ingress, vault-binding

## Failure trigger + adoption signal
- Failure: secrets/support left manual -> teams bypass with copy-pasted infra
- Adoption metric: % of new services created via the path (deploy-log label)
- Reviewer objection: "is this proven or just described?" -> dry-run outputs above
steps: The journey + the hard constraint: The path is defined by its endpoints (empty repo to served/owned/observed) and one non-negotiable: no team writes raw K8s or Terraform. That constraint is what forces the road to stay paved to the last mile.
Template + CI/CD + env — the easy 80%: Backstage scaffolds the repo, the pipeline, and a Terraform namespace. This is the part every 'portal' gets right and mistakes for the whole job.
Secrets + support — the suspect edge: Vault binding and a named on-call are wired BY the path, not left to the team. This is the exact 20% whose absence causes the bypass failure from the diagram.

The inspection hooks — proof, not vibes: helm template piped into kubectl apply --dry-run=server proves the manifests are valid server-side; terraform plan proves the environment actually provisions. These are the two hooks the lesson demands as evidence.

Failure trigger + the adoption metric: The packet names its own failure (manual secrets -> bypass) AND the signal that would expose it: percentage of new services created via the path, read from deploy-log labels. Existence is not the metric; adoption is.

storyboard.say: A developer starts with an empty repo and one click into the Backstage portal — the single entry point to the golden path.
The portal scaffolds a service template — an opinionated default that turns an empty repo into a real service skeleton.
The template wires a CI/CD pipeline automatically, then deploys into a Terraform-provisioned environment — paved by default.
Here is the suspect edge: the running environment needs secrets and an on-call support path — and the template leaves that gap unwired.
When secrets and support are complete, the service flows into observability — a running, observed, owned request.
But if that path is incomplete, teams route around the platform — copy-pasting last year's Terraform. That bypass is the blast radius.
The lesson: pave the whole road end to end as one default, and measure the platform by adoption, not by existence.

# Golden Path: HTTP Service (paved road v1)
## Context
- Journey: empty repo -> first request served + owned + observed, target < 30 min
- Constraint (non-negotiable): NO team hand-writes Kubernetes YAML or Terraform

## Template contract (what `backstage scaffold http-service` guarantees)
- [x] Repo + Dockerfile + Helm chart (helm template renders clean)
- [x] CI/CD: build -> test -> deploy, no per-team pipeline authoring
- [x] Env: Terraform-provisioned namespace + ingress (terraform plan)
- [x] Secrets: Vault path auto-bound to the namespace (NOT left to team)
- [x] Observability: OpenTelemetry SDK + default SLO dashboard on day one
- [x] Support: CODEOWNERS + on-call rotation named at scaffold time

## Inspection proofs (attach outputs)
$ helm template ./chart | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -
  service/orders configured (dry run)
  deployment.apps/orders configured (dry run)
$ terraform plan
  Plan: 3 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy   # namespace, ingress, vault-binding

## Failure trigger + adoption signal
- Failure: secrets/support left manual -> teams bypass with copy-pasted infra
- Adoption metric: % of new services created via the path (deploy-log label)
- Reviewer objection: "is this proven or just described?" -> dry-run outputs above

adoption-metrics.outcome: Take a real (or realistic) internal platform your org ships — a golden path with a service template, CI/CD, environments, and a Backstage portal — and define its adoption metrics: the ONE leading number that proves teams actually use the path (not just that the portal exists), plus the guardrail number that catches teams silently bypassing it.
adoption-metrics.proof: The Adoption section of platform_golden_path_review_packet.md: a scorecard with (1) a golden-path adoption rate with a named numerator/denominator, (2) a bypass/leakage signal, (3) a source for each metric, and (4) one target with a review date. A peer reads it and can tell you whether the platform is winning or being routed around — without you narrating.
adoption-metrics.unlock: Your scorecard measures a behavior teams perform (services created VIA the golden path), separates it from a vanity count (portal page-views), and names one metric that fires when teams bypass the path.
adoption-metrics.doNotClaim: Do not claim "the platform is adopted" from a portal existing, a Backstage catalog being populated, or a launch announcement. A registered service that was hand-rolled around your template is a bypass, not an adoption. If your top metric can go up while teams quietly build infrastructure by hand, it is a vanity metric — replace it.

adoption-metrics.text: The platform team demos a beautiful Backstage portal and a one-click golden path; leadership funds another quarter. Six weeks later a product team ships a new service — hand-written Terraform, copy-pasted CI, secrets pasted into a Slack DM — because the template was missing an environment and nobody could tell, from any dashboard, that the golden path had just been bypassed.

Treating the platform as a product means proving teams adopt the golden path, not that a portal was launched. Adoption metrics are Section-4 evidence in your review packet: the number that separates "we built a paved road" from "traffic actually drives on it."

adoption-metrics.prompt: Your platform dashboard shows 340 services registered in the Backstage catalog and portal visits up 60% this month. Is the golden path being adopted? Answer before reading on.
adoption-metrics.reveal: Unknown — and probably a trap. Catalog registration and portal visits measure presence and curiosity, not the behavior you care about: services created and deployed THROUGH the golden path template. A team can register a hand-rolled service in Backstage and never touch your template. The adoption number that matters is a rate — golden-path-provisioned services ÷ all new services — paired with a bypass signal. A raw count that only goes up hides the teams routing around you, which is exactly the failure this skill exists to catch: the platform creates a portal but teams bypass it because templates, environments, secrets, and support paths are incomplete.

adoption-metrics.code:
## 4. Adoption Scorecard  (golden path: node-svc-template v3)
# Leading metric — the BEHAVIOR, not the portal
golden_path_adoption_rate = svcs_provisioned_via_template / all_new_svcs_this_qtr
  = 11 / 17 = 0.65   target: >= 0.80 by 2026-09-30
  source: Backstage scaffolder `scaffolded` events joined to Terraform Cloud run tags (module=platform/*)

# Guardrail — catches the bypass this failure mode is famous for
bypass_signal = new_svcs_with_offtemplate_terraform / all_new_svcs
  = 6 / 17 = 0.35   alert if > 0.20
  source: repo scan for *.tf NOT importing registry.internal/modules/platform/*

# Health of the path itself (adoption follows time-to-first-deploy)
p50_time_to_first_deploy = 38 min   target: <= 30 min
  source: template scaffold ts -> first successful CI/CD deploy ts

# Trust / retention — do teams STAY on the path after service #2?
second_service_retention = teams_using_path_twice / teams_using_path_once
  = 0.55   watch: < 0.60 means the path is a one-time novelty
  source: golden_path adoption events grouped by owning team
steps: The leading metric is a RATE of a behavior: Numerator: services actually provisioned through the template. Denominator: all new services — including the ones that bypassed you. A raw count of template runs can never expose leakage; a rate can.

Every metric names its source: Backstage scaffolder events JOINED to Terraform Cloud run tags. If you cannot name where the number comes from, a reviewer cannot audit it and neither can you — that is a vanity metric by construction.

The bypass signal is the whole point: 35% of new services carry off-template Terraform — the platform is being routed around. This is the direct instrument for "teams bypass it because the path is incomplete." Alert threshold makes it operational, not decorative.
Bypass source is a concrete scan, not a vibe: Grep for *.tf that does NOT import your platform module registry. Observable and executable — a reviewer can re-run it.
A driver metric, not a vanity one: Time-to-first-deploy is the lever: adoption follows when the path is faster than hand-rolling. 38 min > 30 min target explains WHY 6 teams bypassed.

Retention separates a launch from a product: Second-service retention catches the platform that wins a service once via mandate, then gets abandoned. 0.55 is the honest signal that the path is a novelty, not a habit.

storyboard.say: It starts with a product developer. When they open the Backstage portal, that's just browsing — a page view, not adoption.
The real golden path begins when the developer scaffolds a service from the template — this is the paved road we actually want traffic on.
The template wires up the golden CI/CD pipeline, which then applies the standard Terraform and Kubernetes provisioning.
At provisioning, the golden path emits a real adoption event into the scorecard — this is the behavior we measure, not a page view.
But when the template is missing a piece, the developer bypasses it — hand-rolled Terraform, copy-pasted CI, path incomplete.
That hand-rolled service still registers in the Backstage catalog, and the catalog inflates the raw service count.
So the scorecard sees two inputs: genuine golden-path events and inflated catalog counts. Divide path-scaffolded by all new services, and pair it with a leakage signal.
The lesson: a metric that climbs while teams route around you is vanity — measure the road driven on, and catch the bypass.

ci-cd-contract.proof: platform_golden_path_review_packet.md with a stage/gate table for the CI/CD Contract, the rejected option (and why it fails under real teams), a verification method backed by an inspection hook (kubectl apply --dry-run=server, terraform plan, or helm template), one reviewer objection answered, and a transfer note. A second engineer can read the contract and predict exactly what happens when they push code — without asking you.

ci-cd-contract.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a CI/CD Contract if teams can hand-edit the pipeline freely. A pipeline every team rewrites is not a contract — it is a suggestion. And do not claim it is proven from a green checkmark alone: a passing run with no dry-run/plan gate proves the YAML parsed, not that the deploy is safe.

ci-cd-contract.text: Your platform ships a shiny Backstage portal and a service template. Six weeks later three teams have copy-pasted the generated pipeline and quietly deleted the policy gate — because it was slow and nobody said they couldn't. The portal is adopted; the contract is gone.

A service template's real payload is not the scaffolded folders — it is the CI/CD Contract: the promise that every service built from it is tested, scanned, provisioned, and deployed the same inspectable way. This is lesson 2 of the module; it takes the template you generated in lesson 1 and makes its pipeline a contract teams inherit rather than a starting point they diverge from.

ci-cd-contract.prompt: You give every team a starter pipeline file inside the generated repo, then let them own it. Six months later, why do half of them no longer pass security scans? Answer before reading on.
ci-cd-contract.reveal: Because a starter you hand over is forked, not inherited. The moment the scan slows a Friday deploy, someone comments it out — and now there is no single place to fix it. A CI/CD Contract inverts ownership: the stages and gates live in a centrally-versioned template (a reusable workflow, a shared Terraform module) that services *reference*, not *copy*. Teams get an escape hatch that is logged and reviewable, so a bypass is a visible event, not a silent drift. The failure this lesson exists to kill — the platform creates a portal but teams bypass it because templates, environments, secrets, and support paths are incomplete — starts exactly here: at a pipeline you gave away instead of a contract you kept.

ci-cd-contract.intro: The contract as a reusable workflow teams reference. Trace the complete platform artifact before implementing its deterministic evidence model.
ci-cd-contract.code:
# Generated into every service from the template. The team owns THIS file,
# but the stages + gates live in the platform's reusable workflow it calls.
name: golden-path-delivery
on: { push: { branches: [main] } }

jobs:
  deliver:
    uses: acme-platform/.github/workflows/delivery-contract.yml@v3
    with:
      service: orders-api
      environment: staging
      coverage_min: 80          # gate 1: build + test
      policy_bundle: acme/base  # gate 2: OPA policy + trivy scan
    secrets: inherit            # env + registry creds, platform-managed

  # The ONLY sanctioned bypass. Not a deleted line — a reviewed, logged event.
  break_glass:
    if: contains(github.event.head_commit.message, '[break-glass]')
    uses: acme-platform/.github/workflows/break-glass.yml@v3
    with:
      reason_required: true     # PR must name an approver + expiry
      audit_sink: platform-audit-log
steps: Inherit, do not copy: uses: ...@v3 references the platform's contract by version tag. When the platform hardens a gate, every service that pins @v3 (or floats to it) gets it — there is no per-team fork to chase. This one line is the difference between a contract and a starter.

The gates, passed as data: coverage_min and policy_bundle are inputs, not logic teams can rewrite. The gate implementation stays in the platform; the team declares the values it must meet. This is where terraform plan and the trivy scan run — each able to return 'no' and fail the deploy.

Secrets by inheritance: secrets: inherit means the team never sees registry or env credentials — the incomplete-secrets failure mode from the module scenario is closed by construction, not by a wiki page.

The escape hatch, not a deleted gate: A commit tagged [break-glass] does not remove the scan — it routes through a second workflow that DEMANDS a reason, an approver, and an expiry. The bypass becomes a visible, expiring, audited event.

The audit sink is the proof: audit_sink writes every bypass to platform-audit-log. This is your adoption/drift evidence: a contract with zero break-glass entries is trusted; one with silent scan-deletions is impossible, because deletion is no longer a code path.

The escape hatch routes bypasses through review, not around it. Portal, docs, and non-golden paths are out of scope here.

storyboard.say: A single git push into a templated service triggers the same reusable workflow every service inherits — one entry point, not a copy.
The workflow runs five fixed stages. First, Build and Test: code must compile and pass before anything moves forward.
On pass it reaches the Policy and Security Scan — the one gate designed to say no, and the first one teams quietly delete because it's slow.
Clear the scan and the pipeline plans infrastructure as a dry-run, then deploys that same inspectable way into the environment.
When someone genuinely must bypass the scan, the escape hatch routes it through an audit log — the bypass becomes a visible event.
The hatch resumes the pipeline at plan, recorded — so a skip flows through review, never silently around it.
The template's real payload is this contract: every service tested, scanned, and deployed identically, versioned centrally, with bypass auditable — not a starting point to diverge from.

    uses: acme-platform/.github/workflows/break-glass.yml@v3
    with:
      reason_required: true     # PR must name an approver + expiry
      audit_sink: platform-audit-log

steps.label: Inherit, do not copy
steps.note: uses: ...@v3 references the platform's contract by version tag. When the platform hardens a gate, every service that pins @v3 (or floats to it) gets it — there is no per-team fork to chase. This one line is the difference between a contract and a starter.

steps.label: The gates, passed as data
steps.note: coverage_min and policy_bundle are inputs, not logic teams can rewrite. The gate implementation stays in the platform; the team declares the values it must meet. This is where terraform plan and the trivy scan run — each able to return 'no' and fail the deploy.

steps.label: Secrets by inheritance
steps.note: secrets: inherit means the team never sees registry or env credentials — the incomplete-secrets failure mode from the module scenario is closed by construction, not by a wiki page.

steps.label: The escape hatch, not a deleted gate
steps.note: A commit tagged [break-glass] does not remove the scan — it routes through a second workflow that DEMANDS a reason, an approver, and an expiry. The bypass becomes a visible, expiring, audited event.

steps.label: The audit sink is the proof
steps.note: audit_sink writes every bypass to platform-audit-log. This is your adoption/drift evidence: a contract with zero break-glass entries is trusted; one with silent scan-deletions is impossible, because deletion is no longer a code path.

left.label: Starter pipeline (described)
lines: Constraint: unstated — 'teams should follow the pipeline'
Pipeline copied INTO each repo; teams own + edit it
Scan gate present but deletable, no record if removed
Secrets: 'see onboarding doc' — the incomplete path
Verification: 'the workflow is green' (parsed ≠ safe)
Rejected option + failure mode: not recorded
left.verdict: Adopted on day 1, bypassed by month 2 — no evidence it drifted

right.label: CI/CD Contract (proven)
lines: Constraint named: no daytime downtime; every deploy scanned
Stages + gates inherited via reusable workflow @v3 (referenced)
Scan gate un-deletable; bypass = logged, expiring break-glass
Secrets: inherit — team never holds creds, path complete
Verification: terraform plan + kubectl --dry-run=server clean
Rejected: per-team Jenkinsfiles — fail because drift is invisible

ci-cd-contract.caption: The tell is ownership of the gate. If a team can delete the scan and no one sees it, you shipped a starter and called it a platform. The contract makes divergence a reviewable event, not silent rot.

ci-cd-contract.text: The senior platform move is to treat the platform as a product and the escape hatch as a feature, not a leak. A golden path with no break-glass either has zero adoption or invisible bypasses — both are failure. ci-cd-contract.question: A reviewer asks: 'You gave every team a pipeline with a security-scan step. Prove this is a CI/CD Contract and not just a starter file.' Which answer actually proves it?
options: 'Every repo generated from the template contains the scan step, so it's standard.'

'The scan gate lives in a versioned reusable workflow that services reference, not copy; teams cannot silently delete it, and the only bypass is a logged, expiring break-glass job — here are the audit-log entries.'
'All the pipelines are currently green, so the scans are passing.'
'We documented in the developer portal that teams must keep the scan step enabled.'
ci-cd-contract.explanation: Only option 2 shows the property that makes it a contract: the gate is inherited by reference (not a copy a team can edit away), bypass is impossible-to-hide (a logged, expiring event), and there is auditable evidence. Option 1 confuses generation with enforcement — a copied step is deletable. Option 3 confuses green-now with enforced-always (nothing stops tomorrow's deletion). Option 4 is a wiki, not a gate; documentation is not a control.

Record what would invalidate the contract: any way a team can ship to the environment WITHOUT passing the gates or logging a bypass. If you find one, the contract has a hole.

rollback-workflow.outcome: Take one real service on your platform's golden path and design its rollback workflow: the exact trigger that fires it, the artifact it reverts to, the verification that says "we are safe again," and the ownership boundary — then break the naive version and repair it.
rollback-workflow.proof: platform_golden_path_review_packet.md with a rollback section: the abort trigger, the last-known-good revision it targets, the executable verification hook (kubectl rollout / helm rollback / terraform plan), the blast radius, and the reviewer objection answered. A teammate can run your rollback from the packet alone, at 3 a.m., without asking you a question.
rollback-workflow.unlock: Your rollback workflow names a concrete trigger, a specific good revision, an executable verification, and who owns the call — and a peer could run it without you.
rollback-workflow.doNotClaim: Do not claim a rollback workflow exists because 'we can redeploy the old image.' Redeploy-on-demand is a hope, not a workflow. A workflow has a trigger that fires without a hero, a target that is already pinned, and a check that proves recovery — or teams will bypass the golden path the first time a release goes bad.

rollback-workflow.text: A templated service ships through the golden path Friday at 5 p.m. By 5:40 error rates are climbing, the on-call opens the runbook, and the rollback section says "revert to the previous version." Which version? Where is it pinned? Who hits the button? The silence is the exact moment a team decides the platform is not worth trusting.

Your service template already generates CI/CD, Kubernetes manifests, and Terraform — the forward path is solved. Rollback is the half every platform skips, and it is why teams quietly route around the golden path: a paved road with no reverse gear is a trap, not a template.

rollback-workflow.prompt: Your Helm-deployed service is failing after a release. The obvious fix: `git revert`, let CI rebuild, redeploy the corrected image. Before you reach for it — what is wrong with that as your rollback workflow? Answer before reading on.
rollback-workflow.reveal: It is a roll-FORWARD wearing rollback's clothes. `git revert` + rebuild is a fresh deploy through the same pipeline that just shipped the break — you inherit its full build-and-test latency (10-20 min) during an active incident, and you are betting the new build is clean. Real rollback points at an artifact that already ran green in production — a pinned image digest, a prior Helm revision — and swings back to it in seconds, no rebuild, no new risk. Rolling forward to fix is a decision; rolling back to safety is a reflex, and only one belongs in the 3 a.m. runbook.

rollback-workflow.code:
## Rollback Workflow — orders-service (golden path v3)
# Trigger (fires WITHOUT a human deciding):
#   error_rate > 2% for 5m  OR  readiness probe failing > 3m  (Prometheus alert -> PagerDuty -> runbook)
# Owner: the deploying team's on-call; platform on-call is backup. No approval needed to revert.

# Last-known-good is PINNED, not searched for at 3 a.m.:
helm history orders-service -n prod            # revision 41 = last green, digest sha256:9a3f...

# Execute rollback (revert to proven revision — no rebuild):
helm rollback orders-service 41 -n prod --wait --timeout 120s

# Verify recovery is REAL, not assumed:
kubectl rollout status deploy/orders-service -n prod    # Progressing -> Complete
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f k8s/orders-service.yaml # config matches good state
# then: error_rate back < 0.5% for 5m on the dashboard

# Blast radius: search catalog serves prior template output; secrets + DB schema UNCHANGED (no migration this release)
# Boundary: if this release ran a schema migration, rollback is NOT safe here -> see migration-reversal runbook
steps: The trigger fires itself: An SLO breach on error_rate or the readiness probe pages the on-call — no human has to notice the graph. A rollback that waits for someone to 'realize' is not a workflow.

Ownership is explicit: The deploying team owns the revert; platform is backup. Naming the owner AND 'no approval needed' is what keeps teams on the golden path — they know they can recover without a meeting.
Last-known-good is pinned, not hunted: `helm history` names revision 41 with its image digest ahead of time. At 3 a.m. you read a number, you do not archaeology your registry.
Revert, do not rebuild: `helm rollback` swings to an already-run revision in seconds — the whole point. No CI, no new build risk during an active incident.
Verify recovery is real: `kubectl rollout status` + a server dry-run + the SLO re-check prove you are actually back — 'it deployed' is not 'it recovered.' Two inspection hooks, both executable.

Blast radius + the boundary that invalidates it: State what is affected AND the condition that breaks the workflow: a schema migration makes naive rollback unsafe. Naming what invalidates your answer is the senior move.

# The rollback section of the review packet, line by line
#
# Mission: Take one real service on your platform's golden path and design its rollback workflow: the exact trigger that fires it, the artifact it reverts to, the verification that says "we are safe again," and the ownership boundary — then break the naive version and repair it.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Point to the exact trigger. If a human has to 'notice' the incident before rollback starts, it is not a workflow yet — wire it to an SLO or probe alert.
# 2. Name the last-known-good revision by number/digest in the packet. If you would have to hunt for it during an incident, pin it now (`helm history` / a pinned image digest).
# 3. Run the verification hook against your service: `kubectl rollout status` and `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f service.yaml` (or `helm rollback --dry-run`). It must return an observable 'recovered' signal, not 'it deployed'.
# 4. Confirm the workflow REVERTS, never rebuilds. If your rollback path re-enters CI/CD to build an image, it inherits the broken pipeline's latency and risk — replace it with a revert to a proven artifact.
# 5. State the boundary that invalidates rollback: a schema migration, a secrets rotation, or any irreversible side effect this release performed. If you cannot name what makes reverting unsafe, you have not checked.
#
# Work only in the TODO function. Run every fixture and compare every output line.
# Local execution is practice feedback; it does not create controlled mastery evidence.

RELEASES = [
    # (rev, status, digest, ran_migration)  — helm history, oldest first
    (38, "green",  "sha256:11aa", False),
    (39, "green",  "sha256:22bb", False),
    (40, "failed", "sha256:33cc", False),
    (41, "green",  "sha256:44dd", False),
    (42, "failed", "sha256:55ee", False),
    (43, "green",  "sha256:66ff", True),   # v3.0 — ran a schema migration
    (44, "green",  "sha256:77aa", False),
    (45, "failed", "sha256:88bb", False),  # current — paging right now
]

TRIGGER = {"error_rate_pct": 3.4, "threshold_pct": 2.0, "window_min": 5}

def decide(releases, trigger):
    # TODO: implement the platform decision from the supplied delivery fixtures.
    # Preserve failure discrimination and the exact observable contract.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the platform evidence decision")

fired, current, target, migs, safe = decide(RELEASES, TRIGGER)
print(f"trigger: error_rate {TRIGGER['error_rate_pct']}% > {TRIGGER['threshold_pct']}% for {TRIGGER['window_min']}m -> {'FIRED' if fired else 'quiet'}")
print(f"current: rev {current[0]} ({current[1]})")
print(f"last_known_good: rev {target[0]} digest {target[1]}")
print(f"migrations_since_target: {len(migs)}")
if safe:
    print(f"action: helm rollback orders-service {target[0]} -n prod --wait")
else:
    print("action: BLOCKED — schema migrated since target; use migration-reversal runbook")
print(f"safe_to_rollback: {'yes' if safe else 'NO'}")

rollback-workflow.subtitle: Release promotes through the template's pipeline; a health gate watches the new revision. On breach it reverts to the pinned last-known-good Helm revision and re-verifies. Roll-forward (rebuild) is the OTHER path — deliberately not the incident path.

storyboard.say: It's Friday at 5 p.m. The CI/CD pipeline promotes a templated service through the golden path, pushing an immutable image digest to the registry.
A brand-new revision N goes live. Its image digest is already pinned in the registry, so nothing here has to be rebuilt to move it.
The health gate watches revision N as real traffic hits it. This is the signal that decides whether the release stays or goes.
By 5:40 error rates are climbing. On breach, the gate fires the revert automatically, no human guessing which version to roll back to.
It swings back to last-known-good, revision N-minus-one: an already-run, immutable Helm revision. Fast because it swings, it does not rebuild.
Verify recovery runs the command that proves the service is healthy again, turning rollback from a hope into a checked, boring outcome.
Rolling forward with a rebuilt fix is the other path, done later and off-incident. The invariant: rollback reverts to proven state, never rebuilds.

rollback-workflow.question: A reviewer challenges: "prove your rollback workflow is usable, not just described." Which packet earns the unlock?
options: "On failure, git revert the release commit, let CI rebuild, and redeploy the corrected image."
"error_rate>2%/5m pages on-call; helm rollback to pinned revision 41; kubectl rollout status + SLO re-check confirm recovery; unsafe if this release ran a schema migration."
"The team will roll back to the last stable version using their normal process."
"We have blue-green, so rollback is automatic and we never need a runbook."
rollback-workflow.explanation: Only option 2 is a workflow: a self-firing trigger (SLO breach), a pinned last-known-good target (revision 41, no live hunt), an executable verification (rollout status + SLO), and a stated boundary that invalidates it (a migration). Option 1 rolls FORWARD through the broken pipeline; option 3 hand-waves 'normal process'; option 4 confuses a deploy strategy with a runbook and skips the boundary where blue-green still cannot undo a migration.

items: Point to the exact trigger. If a human has to 'notice' the incident before rollback starts, it is not a workflow yet — wire it to an SLO or probe alert.

Run the verification hook against your service: `kubectl rollout status` and `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f service.yaml` (or `helm rollback --dry-run`). It must return an observable 'recovered' signal, not 'it deployed'.

Confirm the workflow REVERTS, never rebuilds. If your rollback path re-enters CI/CD to build an image, it inherits the broken pipeline's latency and risk — replace it with a revert to a proven artifact.

State the boundary that invalidates rollback: a schema migration, a secrets rotation, or any irreversible side effect this release performed. If you cannot name what makes reverting unsafe, you have not checked.

iac-module-design.proof: platform_golden_path_review_packet.md with a module boundary table (module-owned inputs vs. team-owned inputs), the selected approach, one rejected approach and why it fails on ownership, the bypass-failure trigger, and at least two inspection-hook outputs (terraform plan, kubectl apply --dry-run=server, or helm template). A platform reviewer can point to the exact evidence that the module is used, not just described.
iac-module-design.unlock: Your packet names the module boundary, the ownership split, the bypass failure, and a replayable verification trail — with zero unresolved risk hidden.
iac-module-design.doNotClaim: Do not claim you designed a 'golden path' if your module hard-codes every value and exposes no team-owned inputs. That is a locked box teams route around, not a paved road. And do not claim it is proven from terraform validate alone — validate checks syntax; only plan against real state shows what the module actually creates.

iac-module-design.text: A product team needs to ship a new service by Friday. Without a golden-path module they hand-build a namespace, copy a Terraform file from Slack, paste a secret into an env var, and no one can say who owns the on-call. The platform team's answer to all of it is supposed to be one module — but only if teams reach for it instead of around it.

An internal developer platform lives or dies on adoption: the moment a golden-path module is incomplete on templates, environments, secrets, or support, teams bypass it and the platform becomes shelfware. IaC module design is where you draw the boundary between what the platform owns and what the team owns — the first artifact in Infrastructure & Environments.

iac-module-design.prompt: Your new IaC module provisions the whole service — namespace, ingress, database, secrets, the works — with zero required inputs. Teams should love it, right? Why do they route around it within a week?
iac-module-design.reveal: Because a module that owns everything hides ownership. When it fails, the team can't change the ingress path, rotate the DB secret, or explain why on-call is theirs — so they fork it. A golden path isn't 'we do it all'; it's a contract: the module owns the undifferentiated wiring (network, policy, telemetry hookup), the team owns the differentiated decisions (service name, resource sizing, which secret refs). Hide the seam and adoption dies; the platform ships a portal nobody uses.

iac-module-design.intro: The module contract, one variable at a time. Trace the complete platform artifact before implementing its deterministic evidence model.
iac-module-design.code:
# modules/service/variables.tf — the golden-path CONTRACT
variable "service_name" { type = string }              # TEAM owns
variable "cpu"          { type = string, default = "250m" }  # TEAM tunes
variable "secret_refs"  { type = list(string), default = [] } # TEAM names, not values

# PLATFORM owns the wiring below — not exposed as inputs
locals {
  namespace   = "team-${var.service_name}"
  otel_env    = { OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT = "http://collector:4317" }
  policy_tier = "restricted"  # baseline PodSecurity + NetworkPolicy
}

# Proof, not promises:
#   terraform plan -var service_name=orders
#   kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f rendered.yaml
#   helm template . | opentelemetry-collector validate
steps: Team-owned identity: service_name is the one decision only the team can make. It seeds the namespace — the module owns the derivation, the team owns the name.
Team-owned sizing with a safe default: A golden path defaults so the happy path is one line, but stays tunable so teams don't fork the module to change CPU.

Secret REFERENCES, never values: The module takes secret names, not secret contents. Values live in the external secret store — the module never sees plaintext. This is the ownership seam for secrets.

Platform-owned wiring, hidden on purpose: Namespace convention, OTel endpoint, and the restricted policy tier are locals, not variables. Teams can't misconfigure what they can't reach — cognitive load down, ownership intact.

The verification trail: plan against real state (what does it create?), a server dry-run (does the cluster accept it?), and a telemetry validate (is observability actually wired?). Three inspection hooks a reviewer can replay.

# The module contract, one variable at a time
#
# Mission: Design one IaC module as the golden path for a new service, then produce platform_golden_path_review_packet.md: the module's boundary contract (what it owns vs. what the team owns), the rejected alternative, the failure that makes teams bypass it, and the verification trail (terraform plan + a template dry-run) a reviewer can replay.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Run terraform plan against real state (not just validate). If you only ran validate, you proved syntax, not behavior — re-run with plan.
# 2. Run kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f on the rendered manifest (or helm template): the cluster must accept it, admission policy included.
# 3. Point to the ownership boundary: name at least one team-owned input and one platform-owned local, and confirm secret VALUES never appear in the module — only references.
# 4. Confirm the module attaches observability by default (OpenTelemetry wiring present), so a team gets telemetry without configuring it.
# 5. State the bypass-failure trigger explicitly: what missing piece (template, environment, secret path, or support path) would make a team fork this module — and confirm your packet closes it.
#
# Work only in the TODO function. Run every fixture and compare every output line.
# Local execution is practice feedback; it does not create controlled mastery evidence.

VARIABLES = [
    # (name, side, default)  side: who SHOULD own it per the boundary contract
    ("service_name", "team",     None),
    ("cpu",          "team",     "250m"),
    ("memory",       "team",     "256Mi"),
    ("secret_refs",  "team",     "[]"),
    ("db_password",  "team",     "hunter2"),          # a VALUE, not a reference
    ("otel_endpoint","platform", "http://collector:4317"),  # internal, exposed
    ("policy_tier",  "platform", "restricted"),              # internal, exposed
]

CRED_MARKERS = ("password", "token", "key", "secret_value")

def lint(variables):
    # TODO: implement the platform decision from the supplied delivery fixtures.
    # Preserve failure discrimination and the exact observable contract.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the platform evidence decision")

findings, team_inputs, clean = lint(VARIABLES)
for name, why in findings:
    print(f"{name}: {why}")
print(f"team_inputs: {team_inputs}")
print(f"findings: {len(findings)}")
print(f"boundary: {'CLEAN' if clean else 'LEAKED'}")

storyboard.say: A product team needs to ship a new service, so they start where the platform wants them to: a Backstage template.
Filling that template scaffolds one call to the golden-path IaC module — the single seam between platform-owned and team-owned inputs.
From that one call the module provisions the Kubernetes namespace and deployment, so the team never hand-builds cluster wiring.
It references secrets by pointer, not by value — the team names the ref while the platform owns how secrets are resolved.
And it attaches OpenTelemetry wiring automatically, so observability and on-call ownership are baked in, not bolted on.
But if the module is incomplete on templates, secrets, or support, the team bypasses it and hand-builds a copy pasted from Slack.
The lesson: own the boilerplate and expose the decisions — lower cognitive load without ever hiding ownership or risk.

policy-as-code.code:
package platform.golden_path

# Every service must declare an owning team.
deny[msg] {
  input.kind == "Deployment"
  not input.metadata.labels["platform.io/owner"]
  msg := sprintf("service %q has no platform.io/owner label", [input.metadata.name])
}

# Every container must set CPU + memory limits.
deny[msg] {
  input.kind == "Deployment"
  c := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
  not c.resources.limits.cpu
  msg := sprintf("container %q is missing a CPU limit", [c.name])
}

# No plaintext secrets in env — must come from a secretRef.
deny[msg] {
  input.kind == "Deployment"
  c := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
  e := c.env[_]
  e.value
  contains(lower(e.name), "secret")
  msg := sprintf("container %q sets secret %q inline", [c.name, e.name])
}

storyboard.say: It starts with a developer reaching for the golden-path template — the paved road the platform team built to spin up a new service.
The template pushes into CI, which runs a terraform plan — every change to production flows through this one delivery pipe.
Before anything touches the cluster, CI hands the plan to the policy engine — OPA and Rego evaluate it against the non-negotiable rules.
If the service has an owner, resource limits, and no plaintext secrets, it passes the rules and the engine allows it into production.
But if it violates a single rule, the engine denies it automatically — it never deploys, no polite reminder, just a hard stop.
Compare the dashed path: a wiki standard is unenforced, so teams bypass it and ship straight to the cluster with no guardrail.
The lesson: a portal reminds, but only machine-checked policy where deploys already flow can actually force the golden path.

logging-metrics-traces.proof: platform_golden_path_review_packet.md with an observability section: the template contract line that injects OTel, a metric/log/trace example, the constraint, the rejected approach, the expected failure, and a telemetry check output (`otelcol validate` or a trace showing one request end-to-end). A reviewer can replay one request across all three signals without you narrating.

logging-metrics-traces.doNotClaim: Do not claim the service is observable because you added a logging library. Logs alone answer 'what happened here'; without metrics you cannot answer 'is it healthy at scale', and without a trace you cannot answer 'where in the request did it break'. Three signals or it is not observability — it is print debugging with a shipping label.

logging-metrics-traces.text: A team ships a service off your shiny new portal, it pages at 2 a.m., and the on-call has three tabs open and none of them agree — the logs say 200s, the dashboard says fine, and nobody can see which hop ate the 3 seconds. They stop using your golden path the next morning. The platform did not fail to build; it failed to be observable.

Runtime Platform And Observability is where a golden path proves it is real: a service is only launched if it can be watched. This lesson makes the three signals a template default, so 'observable' is a property of the platform, not a chore each team forgets.

logging-metrics-traces.prompt: A team adds structured logging to their service and calls it 'observable'. Before you agree — what question can logs alone never answer? Decide before reading on.
logging-metrics-traces.reveal: Logs answer 'what happened at this one point'. They cannot answer 'is the whole system healthy right now' — that is a metric, an aggregate over time (p99 latency, error rate, saturation). And they cannot answer 'where across seven services did this one request lose 3 seconds' — that is a trace, a single request stitched across hops by a shared trace ID. logging-metrics-traces.subtitle: A request flows client → gateway → orders → payments, each hop emitting to a shared OTel Collector. The trace stitches the hops by trace_id; metrics aggregate health; logs capture events. The failure path: an UN-instrumented service (payments) is a blind hop no signal can see across.

blind hop — the failure path (bypass)

storyboard.say: A request enters at the client and hits the API Gateway, carrying a trace_id that will identify this one request across every hop.
The gateway propagates that trace context to Orders, so the two hops belong to the same trace instead of two unrelated events.
Every instrumented hop exports the same three signals to a shared OTel Collector: logs for events, metrics for health, spans for the trace.
Here is the failure: Orders calls Payments, but the trace context is dropped, so no signal can stitch across this blind hop.
Payments is un-instrumented and stays silent — no logs, no metrics, no spans — so the three seconds it ate are invisible.
The Collector exports everything it did receive to the backends, but the trace has a hole exactly where the on-call needs to look.
The lesson: make all three signals a template default via OpenTelemetry, so every generated service is born observable — not observable by accident.

service-scaffold.text: A product team wants to launch a new service by Friday. Right now that means three days of copy-pasting another team's Terraform, guessing at secret names, and DM-ing the platform team to ask 'who owns the pipeline?' The golden path is the difference between that and one command that hands them a running, owned, observable service.

Service scaffold is the entry point of the whole internal platform: it is where a request becomes a template, a template becomes provisioned infrastructure, and ownership becomes explicit. Get it wrong and every later platform investment routes around a portal nobody trusts.

service-scaffold.prompt: You ship a beautiful Backstage 'Create Service' button that generates a repo from a template. Adoption stays near zero. Before reading on — why do teams still hand-roll their services?
service-scaffold.reveal: Because the template stopped at the repo. It scaffolded code but left the four things that actually hurt: no environment gets created, secrets are 'figure it out yourself', CI/CD is a broken placeholder, and there is no support path when it breaks. Teams don't bypass the portal because they dislike buttons — they bypass it because the golden path is a golden 20%. A scaffold is only a golden path if it carries template + environment + secrets + pipeline + ownership + support end to end.

service-scaffold.intro: The service template contract — one file that carries the whole path. Trace the complete platform artifact before implementing its deterministic evidence model.
service-scaffold.code:
apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: golden-service
  title: New backend service (golden path)
spec:
  owner: platform-team
  parameters:
    - title: Service basics
      required: [name, owner, tier]
      properties:
        name:  { type: string, pattern: '^[a-z][a-z0-9-]+$' }
        owner: { type: string, description: 'catalog group that OWNS this' }
        tier:  { type: string, enum: [tier-1, tier-2, tier-3] }
  steps:
    - id: scaffold
      action: fetch:template          # repo + Dockerfile + app skeleton
      input: { url: ./skeleton, values: { name: ${{ parameters.name }} } }
    - id: provision
      action: terraform:plan-and-apply # namespace, DB, DNS per tier
      input: { workingDir: ./iac, vars: { tier: ${{ parameters.tier }} } }
    - id: secrets
      action: vault:bind-workload-identity  # NO static keys in repo
      input: { path: secret/${{ parameters.name }} }
    - id: pipeline
      action: github:actions:enable    # build → test → deploy to the new env
    - id: observability
      action: otel:attach-collector    # traces + a starter dashboard
    - id: register
      action: catalog:register         # owner + on-call + runbook link
  output:
    links:
      - title: Service in catalog
        url: ${{ steps.register.output.entityRef }}
steps: Owner is a REQUIRED field: Ownership is not inferred later — the team must name the catalog group that owns this before the service exists. This is the 'does not hide ownership' invariant, enforced at the door.
Tier drives the blast radius: tier-1 vs tier-3 changes how much environment, redundancy, and alerting the scaffold provisions. One field, defensible downstream cost.
Step 1 — scaffold the repo: The visible 20%: code, Dockerfile, app skeleton. If the template stops HERE, you've built the portal teams bypass.
Step 2 — provision the environment: terraform:plan-and-apply creates the namespace, DB, and DNS. The service has somewhere to RUN, not just a repo to sit in.

Step 3 — wire secrets with identity, not static keys: vault:bind-workload-identity means no secret ever lands in the repo. This is the secrets-review gate — a scaffold that writes keys into git is a security incident with a template.
Steps 4-5 — pipeline + observability: CI/CD that actually deploys to the new env, and OpenTelemetry attached from birth. Day-one deploys and day-one traces.
Step 6 — register owner + support path: catalog:register records the owner, on-call, and runbook. When it breaks at 2 a.m., there is a name, not a shrug.
service-scaffold.commonMistake: Golden 20% — teams bypass and hand-roll the rest

storyboard.say: A product team wants a service by Friday, so they send one request into the platform's scaffold portal.
That request generates a service template — the single command that stands in for three days of copy-paste.
From that one template, six things a real service needs fan out at once instead of being hand-assembled.
The repair path carries the substance: a Terraform environment and wired secrets, so no one guesses at names.
It also attaches a working CI/CD pipeline and observability, so the service ships and can be watched on day one.
Crucially, it assigns a named owner — the platform lowers cognitive load without hiding who's on the hook.
The failure path is the scaffold that stops at the repo: teams get bare code and hand-roll the rest.
Skip provisioning and ownership and every team bypasses the portal — get this entry point wrong and later platform work routes around it.

service-scaffold.subtitle: A Backstage software-template. Each parameter and step is a promise the golden path keeps for the team.
service-scaffold.code:
apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: golden-service
  title: New backend service (golden path)
spec:
  owner: platform-team
  parameters:
    - title: Service basics
      required: [name, owner, tier]
      properties:
        name:  { type: string, pattern: '^[a-z][a-z0-9-]+$' }
        owner: { type: string, description: 'catalog group that OWNS this' }
        tier:  { type: string, enum: [tier-1, tier-2, tier-3] }
  steps:
    - id: scaffold
      action: fetch:template          # repo + Dockerfile + app skeleton
      input: { url: ./skeleton, values: { name: ${{ parameters.name }} } }
    - id: provision
      action: terraform:plan-and-apply # namespace, DB, DNS per tier
      input: { workingDir: ./iac, vars: { tier: ${{ parameters.tier }} } }
    - id: secrets
      action: vault:bind-workload-identity  # NO static keys in repo
      input: { path: secret/${{ parameters.name }} }
    - id: pipeline
      action: github:actions:enable    # build → test → deploy to the new env
    - id: observability
      action: otel:attach-collector    # traces + a starter dashboard
    - id: register
      action: catalog:register         # owner + on-call + runbook link
  output:
    links:
      - title: Service in catalog
        url: ${{ steps.register.output.entityRef }}

steps.label: Owner is a REQUIRED field
steps.note: Ownership is not inferred later — the team must name the catalog group that owns this before the service exists. This is the 'does not hide ownership' invariant, enforced at the door.

steps.label: Tier drives the blast radius
steps.note: tier-1 vs tier-3 changes how much environment, redundancy, and alerting the scaffold provisions. One field, defensible downstream cost.

steps.label: Step 1 — scaffold the repo
steps.note: The visible 20%: code, Dockerfile, app skeleton. If the template stops HERE, you've built the portal teams bypass.

steps.label: Step 2 — provision the environment
steps.note: terraform:plan-and-apply creates the namespace, DB, and DNS. The service has somewhere to RUN, not just a repo to sit in.

steps.label: Step 3 — wire secrets with identity, not static keys
steps.note: vault:bind-workload-identity means no secret ever lands in the repo. This is the secrets-review gate — a scaffold that writes keys into git is a security incident with a template.

steps.label: Steps 4-5 — pipeline + observability
steps.note: CI/CD that actually deploys to the new env, and OpenTelemetry attached from birth. Day-one deploys and day-one traces.

steps.label: Step 6 — register owner + support path
steps.note: catalog:register records the owner, on-call, and runbook. When it breaks at 2 a.m., there is a name, not a shrug.

service-scaffold.caption: Prove it, don't trust it: run the template and diff the output — six steps must produce repo + env + secrets + pipeline + traces + a catalog entry with an owner. Missing any one and it is a repo generator wearing a golden-path costume.

artifact-promotion.text: The portal says the service is ready, the golden-path badge is green, and the team ships — then paging fires at 2 a.m. because the staging secret was promoted verbatim into prod, unowned. The template moved; the evidence did not.

Artifact promotion is the moment a service leaves the template and enters a real environment, and it is where internal developer platforms quietly break: teams bypass the golden path when environments, secrets, and support paths are incomplete. This packet is the operational evidence that a promotion is safe to trust, and the capstone reuses it unchanged.

artifact-promotion.prompt: Your CI pipeline is green and Backstage shows the golden-path check passing. Is that enough to promote the artifact to prod? Answer before reading on.
artifact-promotion.reveal: No — a green portal proves the template rendered, not that the target environment accepts it. The promotion gate is a dry-run against the destination: `terraform plan` on the prod workspace and `kubectl apply --dry-run=server` on the prod cluster. CI validates the artifact in the abstract; only a server-side dry-run in the real environment can return 'no'. If your gate can only say 'yes', it is portal theater, not proof.

artifact-promotion.code:
# Platform Golden Path Review Packet — orders-service v2.3.0
## Context
- Promoting orders-service from the Backstage template into prod (Kubernetes + Terraform).
## Constraint (non-negotiable)
- No daytime downtime on the checkout path; secrets must be owned, not copied from staging.
## Selected approach
- Gate = server-side dry-run + secrets ownership review, THEN promote.
## Rejected approach
- Promote on green portal badge (CI + Backstage check) alone.  Why rejected: proves template rendered, not that prod accepts it.
## Expected failure
- Staging secret promoted verbatim -> unowned prod secret -> 2 a.m. page, no rollback owner.
## Verification (inspection hooks — rerun to reproduce)
- $ terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars
    Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy   # no destroy = safe
- $ kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f service.yaml
    deployment.apps/orders-service configured (server dry run)  # prod API accepted it
- $ opentelemetry collector config validate --config otel.yaml
    valid   # telemetry ships before promote, not after
## Reviewer objection + response
- "Is this promoted or described?" -> replay the two dry-runs above; both return non-error against prod.
## Repair notes
- Before promote, ask: who OWNS each secret in the target env?  Block on any staging-copied secret.
steps: Constraint before approach: Name the non-negotiable first — no daytime downtime, owned secrets. The expert move is stating the constraint that rules out an option before you name the option.
Selected: a gate that can fail: A server-side dry-run against the PROD API can return 'no'. That is what makes it a gate and not a badge.
Rejected, with the reason: Record the option you rejected and why. 'Promote on green portal' is the exact failure this domain is famous for — the portal exists but teams bypass it.
The failure that invalidates it: Staging secret copied verbatim into prod, unowned. Specific enough to recognize on a pager, not 'something breaks'.
Inspection hooks — the replayable trail: terraform plan (no destroy), kubectl dry-run=server (prod API accepted it), otel config validate. Two+ hooks required; each output is what a reviewer reruns.
Repair = a reusable rule: Not 'be careful' — 'block on any staging-copied secret'. A rule that prevents the whole miss class on the next promotion.

storyboard.say: It starts clean: a service template scaffolds a CI build, and CI hands off one artifact to the promotion gate.
The gate is the moment the service leaves the template and tries to enter a real environment. Everything hinges here.
On the golden path the gate runs a server-side dry-run against staging; only when the environment accepts the artifact does it pass.
Staging then promotes to production on proof — the inspection-hook output a reviewer can rerun travels with it.
But when secrets or ownership are incomplete, teams route around the gate through a manual bypass instead of fixing the environment.
The bypass ships an unowned artifact straight to prod — the staging secret promoted verbatim, and at 2 a.m. the pager fires.
The invariant: the gate must prove the target environment accepts the artifact, not merely that the template rendered.

# Platform Golden Path Review Packet — orders-service v2.3.0
## Context
- Promoting orders-service from the Backstage template into prod (Kubernetes + Terraform).
## Constraint (non-negotiable)
- No daytime downtime on the checkout path; secrets must be owned, not copied from staging.
## Selected approach
- Gate = server-side dry-run + secrets ownership review, THEN promote.
## Rejected approach
- Promote on green portal badge (CI + Backstage check) alone.  Why rejected: proves template rendered, not that prod accepts it.
## Expected failure
- Staging secret promoted verbatim -> unowned prod secret -> 2 a.m. page, no rollback owner.
## Verification (inspection hooks — rerun to reproduce)
- $ terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars
    Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy   # no destroy = safe
- $ kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f service.yaml
    deployment.apps/orders-service configured (server dry run)  # prod API accepted it
- $ opentelemetry collector config validate --config otel.yaml
    valid   # telemetry ships before promote, not after
## Reviewer objection + response
- "Is this promoted or described?" -> replay the two dry-runs above; both return non-error against prod.
## Repair notes
- Before promote, ask: who OWNS each secret in the target env?  Block on any staging-copied secret.

steps.label: Constraint before approach
steps.note: Name the non-negotiable first — no daytime downtime, owned secrets. The expert move is stating the constraint that rules out an option before you name the option.

steps.label: Selected: a gate that can fail
steps.note: A server-side dry-run against the PROD API can return 'no'. That is what makes it a gate and not a badge.

steps.label: Rejected, with the reason
steps.note: Record the option you rejected and why. 'Promote on green portal' is the exact failure this domain is famous for — the portal exists but teams bypass it.

steps.label: The failure that invalidates it
steps.note: Staging secret copied verbatim into prod, unowned. Specific enough to recognize on a pager, not 'something breaks'.

steps.label: Inspection hooks — the replayable trail
steps.note: terraform plan (no destroy), kubectl dry-run=server (prod API accepted it), otel config validate. Two+ hooks required; each output is what a reviewer reruns.

steps.label: Repair = a reusable rule
steps.note: Not 'be careful' — 'block on any staging-copied secret'. A rule that prevents the whole miss class on the next promotion.

environment-lifecycle.outcome: Take a real service your platform must support and write the golden-path review packet for its environment lifecycle: how an environment is created, promoted, and destroyed, the one constraint that governs it, the failure you fear when teams route around the portal, and the proof that another reviewer can inspect.
environment-lifecycle.proof: platform_golden_path_review_packet.md with a lifecycle map (create -> promote -> destroy), the selected approach, the rejected approach, an expected failure, a verification method (at least two inspection-hook outputs), a reviewer objection, and a transfer note. A peer reads it and can create AND destroy an environment from your packet without asking you a question.
environment-lifecycle.unlock: Your packet names the constraint, shows the full create-to-destroy lifecycle, and attaches an executable verification (terraform plan / kubectl --dry-run=server) — not a description of one.
environment-lifecycle.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have an environment lifecycle if you only documented how to CREATE an environment. A lifecycle that cannot destroy and reclaim what it created is a leak generator: orphaned namespaces, dangling secrets, and a cloud bill that only grows. Create-only is half a lifecycle wearing the whole name.

environment-lifecycle.text: The platform team ships a beautiful Backstage portal with a 'Create Service' button, takes a victory lap, and three weeks later finds half the teams still hand-crafting namespaces in Slack threads because the portal creates an environment but never tells them how to promote it, rotate its secrets, or tear it down. The portal exists; the lifecycle does not, so the golden path is a demo, not a road.

A service is not a file you write once — it is an environment that is born, promoted through dev to staging to prod, and must eventually die and give its resources back. The environment lifecycle is the golden path made durable: Section 3 of the review packet that turns 'we have a portal' into 'a new team can self-serve a safe environment and reclaim it without a human in the loop.'

environment-lifecycle.prompt: Your platform lets any team click 'Create Environment' and get a namespace, a database, and secrets in ninety seconds. Adoption is high. What is the most expensive thing you probably forgot to build? Answer before reading on.
environment-lifecycle.reveal: Destruction. Creation is the exciting half; teams demand it, so you build it well. But an environment that can be created and never cleanly destroyed accumulates orphaned namespaces, unrotated secrets, and idle Postgres instances — a slow leak that shows up as a cloud bill and a security audit finding, not an outage. The senior move is to build 'create' and 'destroy' as one reversible transaction, so every environment knows how to give itself back.

## 3. Environment Lifecycle (golden path)
# create: `backstage scaffold` -> renders this Terraform module per environment
module "service_env" {
  source      = "platform/service-env/aws"
  name        = var.service_name        # e.g. orders
  tier        = var.tier                # dev | staging | prod
  ttl_hours   = var.tier == "dev" ? 72 : 0   # dev envs self-destruct
  namespace   = "${var.service_name}-${var.tier}"
  secrets_ref = "vault://env/${var.service_name}/${var.tier}"
}
# promote: CI gate must pass before staging -> prod apply
# destroy: `terraform destroy` reclaims namespace + secrets + DB (no orphans)

# --- verification (run BEFORE apply; two inspection hooks) ---
# 1. IaC plan is clean and creates exactly what we expect:
terraform plan -var tier=dev            # expect: 1 namespace, 1 db, 1 secret
# 2. The rendered manifest is valid against the live API server:
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f rendered/orders-dev.yaml

- Selected approach: templated + TTL'd ephemeral envs, destroy in the same module
- Rejected approach: portal creates only; teams delete by hand (orphan leak)
- Expected failure: destroy skips the Vault secret -> stale credential survives
- Reversal condition: TTL sweep + `terraform state list` diff nightly
steps: One template, every tier: The same module renders dev, staging, and prod — the golden path is parameterized, not copy-pasted. `tier` is the one knob that changes behavior.
TTL makes dev self-destruct: Dev environments carry a 72h time-to-live; prod is 0 (never auto-destroys). This is how you prevent the orphan leak by construction, not by nagging teams.

Namespace + secrets bound to the env: The Kubernetes namespace and the Vault secret reference are derived from the same name+tier, so destroy knows exactly what to reclaim. Nothing is created outside the module's knowledge.
terraform plan — inspection hook 1: Before any apply, prove the plan creates EXACTLY one namespace, one DB, one secret. A plan that shows drift or extra resources is the failure caught cheaply.

kubectl --dry-run=server — inspection hook 2: Server-side dry-run validates the rendered manifest against the live API (admission webhooks, quotas) without mutating anything. This is your second falsifiable check.

The expected failure, named: Destroy that reclaims the namespace but skips the Vault secret leaves a live credential behind. Naming this before it happens is what separates the packet from a wiki page.
Reversal condition = the leak detector: A nightly `terraform state list` diff plus TTL sweep catches orphans the module missed. Reversibility is a running check, not a hope.

# The service template that owns the whole lifecycle
#
# Mission: Take a real service your platform must support and write the golden-path review packet for its environment lifecycle: how an environment is created, promoted, and destroyed, the one constraint that governs it, the failure you fear when teams route around the portal, and the proof that another reviewer can inspect.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Run terraform plan on your template and confirm it creates EXACTLY the resources you expect (one namespace, DB, secret per env) — no drift, no extras. Paste the plan into the packet.
# 2. Run kubectl apply --dry-run=server on the rendered manifest and confirm it passes admission and quota checks against the live API without mutating anything.
# 3. Run terraform destroy (or trace it on paper for prod) and confirm every created resource is reclaimed — the namespace, the Vault secret, and the database. If any survives, that orphan is your leak.
# 4. Confirm dev/ephemeral environments carry a TTL or auto-teardown trigger, so an abandoned env destroys itself instead of billing forever.
# 5. Confirm the promotion path (dev -> staging -> prod) is a GATED step, not a hand-copy — name the gate that blocks an unproven build from prod.
# 6. Confirm your packet names one expected failure (e.g. destroy skips the secret) and a reversal condition (a nightly state diff or TTL sweep) that catches it.
#
# Work only in the TODO function. Run every fixture and compare every output line.
# Local execution is practice feedback; it does not create controlled mastery evidence.

ENVIRONMENTS = [
    # (name, tier, age_hours, ttl_hours)   ttl 0 = no expiry
    ("orders-dev-pr114", "dev",     80, 72),
    ("orders-dev-pr118", "dev",     20, 72),
    ("search-dev-spike", "dev",    300, 72),
    ("orders-staging",   "staging",900,  0),
    ("orders-prod",      "prod",  2100,  0),
]

# what the module RECORDS as belonging to each env (terraform state)
STATE = {
    "orders-dev-pr114": ["namespace", "database", "vault_secret"],
    "orders-dev-pr118": ["namespace", "database", "vault_secret"],
    "search-dev-spike": ["namespace", "database", "vault_secret"],
    "orders-staging":   ["namespace", "database", "vault_secret"],
    "orders-prod":      ["namespace", "database", "vault_secret"],
}

# what the destroy step ACTUALLY tears down today
DESTROY_HANDLES = ["namespace", "database"]   # vault_secret missing!

def sweep(envs, state, destroy_handles):
    # TODO: implement the platform decision from the supplied delivery fixtures.
    # Preserve failure discrimination and the exact observable contract.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the platform evidence decision")

expired, orphans = sweep(ENVIRONMENTS, STATE, DESTROY_HANDLES)
for name, tier, age, ttl in expired:
    print(f"expire: {name} (age {age}h > ttl {ttl}h)")
for name, res in orphans:
    print(f"ORPHAN: {name} leaves '{res}' alive after destroy")
print(f"expired: {len(expired)}, orphaned_resources: {len(orphans)}")
print(f"lifecycle: {'CLEAN' if not orphans else 'LEAKING'}")
