storyboard.say: It starts with one service template — the golden path made durable, so a new team scaffolds an environment the same safe way every time.
Create provisions the first tier: a dev environment, born from the template with its own namespace and secrets.
When a PR merges, the dev environment hits the promote gate — the tier boundary a service must cross to advance.
If the gate passes, promotion mints the prod environment — same shape, higher stakes, still governed by the template.
Every environment must eventually die: dev on a closed PR or TTL, prod on decommission — both flow into destroy.
Destroy is the suspect edge: if reclaim fails, namespaces and secrets orphan — the blast radius of a create-only portal.
The invariant: anything the platform can create, it must cleanly destroy. Create-only is a leak, not a lifecycle.

environment-lifecycle.title: The service template that owns the whole lifecycle
environment-lifecycle.subtitle: A Backstage software template plus its Terraform module — create and destroy as one reversible contract, dry-run verified before it ever touches a cluster.
environment-lifecycle.code:
## 3. Environment Lifecycle (golden path)
# create: `backstage scaffold` -> renders this Terraform module per environment
module "service_env" {
  source      = "platform/service-env/aws"
  name        = var.service_name        # e.g. orders
  tier        = var.tier                # dev | staging | prod
  ttl_hours   = var.tier == "dev" ? 72 : 0   # dev envs self-destruct
  namespace   = "${var.service_name}-${var.tier}"
  secrets_ref = "vault://env/${var.service_name}/${var.tier}"
}
# promote: CI gate must pass before staging -> prod apply
# destroy: `terraform destroy` reclaims namespace + secrets + DB (no orphans)

# --- verification (run BEFORE apply; two inspection hooks) ---
# 1. IaC plan is clean and creates exactly what we expect:
terraform plan -var tier=dev            # expect: 1 namespace, 1 db, 1 secret
# 2. The rendered manifest is valid against the live API server:
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f rendered/orders-dev.yaml

- Selected approach: templated + TTL'd ephemeral envs, destroy in the same module
- Rejected approach: portal creates only; teams delete by hand (orphan leak)
- Expected failure: destroy skips the Vault secret -> stale credential survives
- Reversal condition: TTL sweep + `terraform state list` diff nightly

steps.label: One template, every tier
steps.note: The same module renders dev, staging, and prod — the golden path is parameterized, not copy-pasted. `tier` is the one knob that changes behavior.

steps.label: TTL makes dev self-destruct
steps.note: Dev environments carry a 72h time-to-live; prod is 0 (never auto-destroys). This is how you prevent the orphan leak by construction, not by nagging teams.

steps.label: Namespace + secrets bound to the env
steps.note: The Kubernetes namespace and the Vault secret reference are derived from the same name+tier, so destroy knows exactly what to reclaim. Nothing is created outside the module's knowledge.

steps.label: terraform plan — inspection hook 1
steps.note: Before any apply, prove the plan creates EXACTLY one namespace, one DB, one secret. A plan that shows drift or extra resources is the failure caught cheaply.

steps.label: kubectl --dry-run=server — inspection hook 2
steps.note: Server-side dry-run validates the rendered manifest against the live API (admission webhooks, quotas) without mutating anything. This is your second falsifiable check.

steps.label: The expected failure, named
steps.note: Destroy that reclaims the namespace but skips the Vault secret leaves a live credential behind. Naming this before it happens is what separates the packet from a wiki page.

steps.label: Reversal condition = the leak detector
steps.note: A nightly `terraform state list` diff plus TTL sweep catches orphans the module missed. Reversibility is a running check, not a hope.

secrets-management.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'managed secrets' because the template no longer prints a password to logs. If the secret is base64 in a committed manifest, or the template hands teams a raw value to paste, you moved the plaintext, you did not manage it. Managed means: never at rest in the repo, brokered at runtime, and revocable.

secrets-management.text: A team adopts your golden path in an afternoon, ships to prod by Friday — and Monday a security scanner flags their DB password sitting in a committed values.yaml, base64-encoded, which everyone read as 'encrypted.' The portal made the wrong thing effortless.

Secrets are the one part of the golden path where a convenient default is a breach. This is Section 3 of the review packet you carry through the module: the template must hand teams a safe path to credentials that is easier than the unsafe one — or teams bypass the platform exactly here.

secrets-management.prompt: A teammate says the DB password is safe because it is stored as a Kubernetes Secret and everything in etcd is 'encrypted at rest.' Before reading on — what is wrong with treating that as done?
secrets-management.reveal: base64 is not encryption, and a Kubernetes Secret is base64 by default. `kubectl get secret -o yaml` prints it in plaintext to anyone with read access, and if that manifest is in git the value is in history forever. 'Encrypted at rest' describes the disk, not the object — RBAC, a real KMS/broker, and keeping it out of the repo are the actual controls. Calling it done is the false confidence the weak version trades on.

secrets-management.intro: The golden-path template, one secret reference at a time. Trace the complete platform artifact before implementing its deterministic evidence model.
secrets-management.code:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: orders-db
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h            # re-pull so rotation propagates
  secretStoreRef:
    name: vault-backend          # broker, not the repo
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: orders-db-secret       # synced K8s Secret, RBAC-scoped
  data:
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef:
        key: platform/orders/db   # a NAME, never a value
        property: password
---
# Deployment consumes by reference — plaintext never appears here
env:
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: orders-db-secret
        key: password
steps: refreshInterval: The template re-pulls hourly so a rotation in the broker reaches the pod without a redeploy — this is what makes the secret revocable, the whole point.
Point at the broker, not the repo: secretStoreRef names Vault (a ClusterSecretStore). The credential's source of truth lives outside git. This is the accent edge from the diagram.
Reference by name only: remoteRef.key is `platform/orders/db` — a path in the broker. No password, no base64 blob. `git grep` for a secret value returns nothing by construction.
Consume by reference: The Deployment mounts the synced Secret via secretKeyRef. The pod sees the value at runtime; the manifest, and therefore git, never does.

# The golden-path template, one secret reference at a time
#
# Mission: Take the golden-path service template your platform ships and decide how it hands teams their secrets. Produce platform_golden_path_review_packet.md: the operating constraint, the selected secrets approach, the rejected approach, the failure you fear, an executable verification, and a reviewer objection you answered.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. `git grep -iE 'password|secret|BEGIN .*PRIVATE KEY|[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}='` across the template returns nothing that is an actual credential value.
# 2. `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f secrets.yaml` validates the ExternalSecret and Deployment refs against the live API, and `terraform plan` shows the broker/store wiring with no plaintext in the plan output.
# 3. Name the rejected approach (raw Kubernetes Secret in git) and the exact result that disqualifies it — a scanner or `kubectl get secret -o yaml` reveals the value.
# 4. Demonstrate revocability: rotate the value in the broker and confirm the pod picks it up on refresh without a code change or redeploy.
# 5. Confirm read access is scoped: RBAC limits which namespaces/service accounts can read the synced Secret — 'who can read it' has a named answer, not 'anyone with cluster access'.
#
# Work only in the TODO function. Run every fixture and compare every output line.
# Local execution is practice feedback; it does not create controlled mastery evidence.

import base64

FILES = {
    "values.yaml": [
        "replicas: 3",
        "dbPassword: aHVudGVyMi1wcm9k",          # base64 — NOT encryption
        "image: registry/orders:1.4.2",
    ],
    "secrets.yaml": [
        "kind: ExternalSecret",
        "remoteRef: platform/orders/db",           # a NAME — safe
    ],
    "deploy.env": [
        "STRIPE_TOKEN=sk_live_9f8g7h6j5k4l",       # plaintext credential
        "LOG_LEVEL=info",
    ],
    ".git-history.bak": [
        "dbPassword: old-hunter2",                  # deleted, still in history
    ],
}

def looks_base64_secret(value):
    if len(value) < 12:
        return False
    try:
        decoded = base64.b64decode(value, validate=True).decode()
    except Exception:
        return False
    return any(c.isalpha() for c in decoded)

    # Preserve failure discrimination and the exact observable contract.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the platform evidence decision")

findings = scan(FILES)
for fname, key, why in findings:
    print(f"{fname}: {key} -> {why}")
print(f"findings: {len(findings)}")

secrets-management.title: How the golden path brokers a secret — the failure path and the repair path
secrets-management.subtitle: Two ways the template can wire the same DB credential. The dashed red edge is the failure the reviewer replays; the green path is the repair. Payments and billing are out of scope.

legend.label: failure path — secret at rest in the repo
reference by name, no value in git
repair path — brokered + revocable at runtime

storyboard.say: A developer adopts the golden path, needs a DB credential, and reaches the one fork where the convenient default is a breach.
The unsafe path: the developer pastes the password into values.yaml and commits it straight into the git repo.
It looks safe because it's base64-encoded, but base64 is not encryption — anyone with repo access can decode the live credential.
The repair starts here: the developer only names the secret in the service template, never its value.
The template declares a reference, and the External Secrets Operator fetches it from the broker at deploy time.
The broker injects the secret into the pod at runtime, so the credential exists in memory, never in git.
The pod authenticates to Postgres with a rotatable secret — revoke or rotate it anytime, no code change, no git history to scrub.
The invariant: no plaintext or base64 credential in git, every secret rotatable — the safe path made easier than the unsafe one.

kubernetes-abstractions.outcome: Take one real service a product team wants to launch and design its Kubernetes abstraction as a golden-path service template — not a hand-built manifest. Write platform_golden_path_review_packet.md: the constraint, the abstraction you expose (and what you deliberately hide), the rejected option, the failure that makes teams bypass the platform, and the proof that a template-generated service actually deploys.
kubernetes-abstractions.proof: platform_golden_path_review_packet.md: a service-template contract (the fields a team fills vs the Deployment/Service/Ingress/HPA the platform renders), one named non-negotiable constraint, the rejected approach, the bypass-failure mode, and a `kubectl apply --dry-run=server` OR `helm template` output proving the rendered manifests are valid. A peer platform engineer signs that a team could ship a new service through it without writing raw YAML.
kubernetes-abstractions.unlock: Your packet names the abstraction boundary (what the template owns vs what the team owns), attaches a dry-run/render proof, and states the failure that would drive teams off the golden path.
kubernetes-abstractions.doNotClaim: Do not claim you built a Kubernetes abstraction if your template just wraps raw YAML the team still has to edit. Exposing a copy of a Deployment manifest is not an abstraction — it is the same cognitive load with a logo on it. The abstraction is real only when the team declares intent (name, port, replicas, env) and the platform owns the Kubernetes objects.

kubernetes-abstractions.text: A product team needs to launch a new service by Friday. Without a golden path they hand-write a Deployment, a Service, an Ingress, an HPA, a NetworkPolicy, and a secret mount — six objects, forty tunables, one silent typo in the readiness probe — and page you at 2 a.m. when it CrashLoopBackOffs. The whole platform exists to replace that night with a template and one `kubectl apply --dry-run=server`.

This is Runtime Platform And Observability, and Kubernetes abstractions are where boundary and ownership get decided: which Kubernetes objects the platform owns on the team's behalf, and which knobs stay theirs. Get the boundary wrong and teams either drown in YAML or bypass the portal — so the deliverable is a service-template decision packet a reviewer can inspect, not a diagram of pods.

kubernetes-abstractions.prompt: "We'll give every team a copy of a Deployment YAML to edit for their service." Before you build the portal — what is wrong with that as a Kubernetes abstraction? Answer before reading on.
kubernetes-abstractions.reveal: It is not an abstraction — it is copy-paste with extra steps. Handing over raw Deployment/Service/Ingress YAML pushes the full Kubernetes surface (probes, resource limits, securityContext, rollout strategy) onto every product team, so each service drifts and every misconfiguration becomes your page. A real abstraction inverts ownership: the team declares intent (`name`, `image`, `port`, `replicas`, `env`) and the platform renders and owns the objects. The tell you smuggled in the wrong boundary: the team still has to know what a `readinessProbe` is.

kubernetes-abstractions.intro: The service template: intent contract → rendered, dry-run-validated objects. Trace the complete platform artifact before implementing its deterministic evidence model.
kubernetes-abstractions.code:
# service.yaml — the ONLY file a product team writes (the abstraction boundary)
apiVersion: platform.sage.dev/v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  team: payments        # ownership is declared, never hidden
spec:
  image: registry/checkout-api:1.4.2
  port: 8080
  replicas: { min: 3, max: 10 }   # platform renders an HPA from this
  env:
    - name: DATABASE_URL
      fromSecret: checkout-db      # secret path, not the secret value
  healthcheck: /healthz           # platform renders readiness + liveness probes
# --- everything below is rendered + OWNED by the platform, not the team ---
# Deployment (probes, resource limits, securityContext, rollout strategy)
# Service + Ingress (routing, TLS)
# HorizontalPodAutoscaler (from replicas.min/max)
# OpenTelemetry sidecar + ServiceMonitor (observability, auto-attached)

# Inspection hooks — proof the golden path renders VALID Kubernetes:
#   helm template ./golden-path -f service.yaml            # render the objects
#   kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f rendered.yaml        # validate server-side
#   terraform plan                                         # namespace + RBAC + secret refs
steps: Ownership is declared, not hidden: name + team make boundary and ownership inspectable. The platform lowers cognitive load; it does not obscure who owns the service.
The intent surface: image and port are the team's real decisions. This is the whole abstraction: five fields instead of six raw Kubernetes objects.
replicas → HPA (platform-owned): The team says min/max; the platform renders the HorizontalPodAutoscaler. The team never writes autoscaling YAML — that is the point of the abstraction.
Secrets by reference, never by value: fromSecret names a path; the raw secret never enters the team's file. Incomplete secret handling is a top reason teams bypass the portal — so it is first-class.
healthcheck → probes (platform-owned): One path renders both readiness and liveness probes. The team never has to know a readinessProbe exists — the cognitive load the golden path removes.

The proof, not a promise: helm template renders; kubectl apply --dry-run=server validates against the live API; terraform plan proves namespace/RBAC/secret refs. Two hooks minimum — this is the verification trail a reviewer replays.

storyboard.say: It starts with the product team, who need to launch a service by Friday without hand-writing six Kubernetes objects and forty tunables.
The team fills a small contract: service.yaml declares only name, image, port, replicas, and env — the knobs that are genuinely theirs.

The dashed path is the failure to prevent: if the template, secrets, or env are incomplete, the team hand-writes YAML and bypasses the portal.

kubernetes-abstractions.intro: Prove your golden path holds — template contract, provisioning dry-run, secrets, observability:
items: Run `helm template ./golden-path -f service.yaml` and confirm it renders a Deployment, Service, and HPA the team never had to write by hand.
Run `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f rendered.yaml` and confirm every rendered object is valid against the live API — not just YAML-parseable.
Check the abstraction boundary is defensible: name at least one Kubernetes object the platform owns and one field the team owns, and confirm no raw Deployment YAML leaks into the team's surface.
Confirm secrets are referenced by path (fromSecret), never inlined — incomplete secret handling is a top reason teams bypass the portal.
Confirm observability is attached by default (OpenTelemetry sidecar / ServiceMonitor rendered), so a new service emits traces and metrics without the team remembering to add them.

State the invalidation condition: what would make this look acceptable in review but fail when boundary and ownership change (e.g. a team needing a knob the template can't express and hand-writing YAML around it).

slo-defaults.outcome: Take one service on your golden path and ship SLO defaults it inherits by construction: a named SLI, a default target and error budget baked into the service template, and the alert + burn-rate policy that fires on the budget — not on raw CPU. Then write the decision packet that defends why these defaults fit before a team overrides them.
slo-defaults.proof: platform_golden_path_review_packet.md with: the SLI definition (what a good event is), the default SLO target + 30-day error budget, the burn-rate alert policy, the rejected alternative, the failure trigger, and one reviewer objection answered. A peer scaffolds a new service from the template and gets working SLOs + alerts with zero hand-built observability.
slo-defaults.unlock: Your default SLO is inherited from the template (not hand-wired per team), targets an error budget, and is defended against one reviewer objection.
slo-defaults.doNotClaim: Do not claim you shipped SLO defaults if the template only emits a dashboard. A dashboard nobody is paged on is decoration. The default must include an SLI, a budget, and a burn-rate alert that can fire — or teams silently bypass it and the platform's promise is a lie.

slo-defaults.text: Every team on the platform hand-rolls its own alerts, so at 3 a.m. one service pages on 80% CPU (a non-event) while the checkout service quietly burns its entire month of error budget with nobody watching. The golden path shipped a portal — and every team bypassed its observability.

A platform's promise is 'launch a service without hand-building infrastructure' — and observability is where that promise usually breaks. SLO defaults make reliability a property new services inherit from the template, not a bespoke project each team reinvents (badly) after the first incident.

slo-defaults.prompt: The default alert most platforms ship is 'page when CPU > 80% or error rate > 1%'. Before you accept that — what is wrong with it as a DEFAULT for every service? Answer before reading on.
slo-defaults.reveal: It alerts on causes, not on user pain — and it has no budget. CPU at 80% may be perfectly healthy; 1% errors may be fine for a batch job and catastrophic for checkout. A real default measures an SLI (a good-event ratio users feel), sets an SLO target, derives an error budget from it, and pages on how fast that budget is BURNING. Threshold-on-cause defaults train teams to mute alerts — which is why they bypass the platform.

slo-defaults.intro: The SLO default baked into the template. Trace the complete platform artifact before implementing its deterministic evidence model.
slo-defaults.code:
# slo-defaults.yaml — injected into every service by the golden-path template
apiVersion: sloth.slok.dev/v1
kind: PrometheusServiceLevel
metadata:
  name: {{ service_name }}-slo   # rendered by the Backstage scaffolder
spec:
  service: {{ service_name }}
  slos:
    - name: availability
      objective: 99.9            # DEFAULT target for the "web-api" service class
      # SLI = good events / valid events, from OpenTelemetry HTTP metrics
      sli:
        events:
          errorQuery: sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="{{ service_name }}",code=~"5.."}[5m]))
          totalQuery: sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="{{ service_name }}"}[5m]))
      alerting:
        name: {{ service_name }}HighErrorBudgetBurn
        pageAlert:   { labels: { severity: page } }   # fast burn → wake someone
        ticketAlert: { labels: { severity: ticket } }  # slow burn → next business day
# 99.9% over 30d => 43m 12s of error budget. Fast-burn (2%/1h) pages; slow-burn tickets.
steps: Rendered, not hand-written: The service name is templated by the Backstage scaffolder — a team gets this file for free at `create service`, not after their first outage.
The default target is a policy choice: 99.9% is the default for the `web-api` service class. It is opinionated on purpose: a default that means 'pick a number' is no default at all.
SLI = good / valid, from OTel: The SLI is a ratio users feel (non-5xx over total), sourced from the OpenTelemetry metrics the template already wires up — not from CPU.
Two-window burn-rate, not a threshold: Fast burn pages; slow burn opens a ticket. This is the line that stops alert fatigue: you page on how fast the 43-minute budget is being spent.
Prove it before merge: The pipeline runs `kubectl apply --dry-run=server` on the rendered manifest and `otel config validate` on the collector — so a broken SLI can't ship silently.

slo-defaults.starter:
# The SLO default baked into the template
#
# Mission: Take one service on your golden path and ship SLO defaults it inherits by construction: a named SLI, a default target and error budget baked into the service template, and the alert + burn-rate policy that fires on the budget — not on raw CPU. Then write the decision packet that defends why these defaults fit before a team overrides them.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Scaffold a brand-new service from the template and confirm it gets an SLI, an SLO target, and a burn-rate alert with zero hand-editing. If you had to add observability by hand, it is not a default yet.
# 2. Confirm the SLI is a good/valid event ratio sourced from OpenTelemetry — not a CPU or memory threshold dressed up as an SLO.
# 3. Compute the error budget your target implies (99.9% over 30d = 43m 12s) and confirm the alert pages on budget BURN rate, not on a static error percentage.
# 4. Run the pipeline hooks: `kubectl apply --dry-run=server` on the rendered SLO manifest and `otel config validate` on the collector config. Both must pass before merge.
# 5. Inject a fault (return 5xx for a window) and confirm the fast-burn alert actually pages. An alert that never fires in a drill is theatre.
# 6. Confirm a team can override the default with a documented reason — and that the override is captured, so ownership stays visible.
#
# Work only in the TODO function. Run every fixture and compare every output line.
# Local execution is practice feedback; it does not create controlled mastery evidence.

TARGET = 99.9          # % availability, 30-day window
WINDOW_DAYS = 30

# last 6 hours of the checkout service, hourly buckets:
HOURS = [
    # (hour, errors, total_requests)
    ("h-1", 12,   120000),
    ("h-2", 9,    118000),
    ("h-3", 3100, 122000),   # incident window
    ("h-4", 2900, 121000),
    ("h-5", 14,   119000),
    ("h-6", 11,   120500),
]

FAST_BURN = 14.4   # page: burning 30d budget in ~2 days
SLOW_BURN = 3.0    # ticket: burning it in ~10 days

def budget_minutes(target_pct, window_days):
    return window_days * 24 * 60 * (100 - target_pct) / 100

def classify(hours, target_pct):
    # TODO: implement the platform decision from the supplied delivery fixtures.
    # Preserve failure discrimination and the exact observable contract.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the platform evidence decision")

budget = budget_minutes(TARGET, WINDOW_DAYS)
mins = int(budget)
print(f"target: {TARGET}% over {WINDOW_DAYS}d -> error budget {mins}m {int(round((budget - mins) * 60))}s")
for hour, err_frac, burn, level in classify(HOURS, TARGET):
    print(f"{hour}: err {err_frac * 100:.3f}% burn x{burn:.1f} -> {level}")
pages = sum(1 for x in classify(HOURS, TARGET) if x[3] == "PAGE")
print(f"pages: {pages} (both incident hours; the 0.01% hours never fire)")

storyboard.say: Every service starts from one golden-path template — it scaffolds the new service so reliability is inherited, not hand-built later.
The template instruments the service by default: OpenTelemetry ships with it, so no team has to wire up observability from scratch.
The OTel collector feeds the SLI — good events over valid events — which the template pins to an SLO target like ninety-nine point nine percent.
That target implies an error budget, and the SLO exposes how much of that budget remains as the month burns down.
The burn-rate alert watches budget consumption: a fast burn pages on-call immediately, because that means users are actually being hurt.
The trap is CPU and infra alerts firing at eighty percent — a non-event at 3 a.m. — while checkout silently burns its whole budget.
So the default triggers on budget, never on CPU — reliability becomes a property teams inherit, and override only with a stated reason.

slo-defaults.text: The senior platform tell: a good SLO default is one the owning team ARGUES DOWN, not one they ignore. If every team silently accepts 99.9%, your default is probably wrong for half of them and they've stopped reading. A default that provokes 'checkout needs 99.95%, this batch job only needs 99%' is working — it made reliability a decision instead of an accident, and it kept ownership with the team instead of hiding it in the platform.

slo-defaults.question: A reviewer challenges your SLO defaults: 'How is this proven usable, not just described?' Which evidence actually answers the challenge?
options: A slide saying every service now has reliability targets.

A new service scaffolded from the template that emits its SLI from OTel, has a rendered 99.9% SLO with a 30-day budget, fires a burn-rate page in a fault-injection test, and passes dry-run + otel-validate in CI.
A Grafana dashboard screenshot with green panels.
A statement that the default is 99.9% because that is the industry standard.
slo-defaults.explanation: Only option 2 is inspectable proof across the three layers the lesson demands: template contract (scaffolded service), telemetry (SLI from OTel), and an executable check (the burn-rate alert actually fires under fault injection, and CI validates the manifest). Slides (1), a green dashboard nobody is paged on (3), and appeal-to-standard (4) all describe the default without proving a service inherits and enforces it.

storyboard.say: A developer opens the Backstage portal and clicks create — this is the one entry point the platform team wants everyone to use.
The portal generates a service template — the scaffold that's supposed to carry a new service all the way to production.
From the scaffold the paved road runs on: it wires the CI/CD pipeline, which then provisions the environment automatically.
The environment is enforced by a policy gate, which then wires secrets and instruments observability — every stage paved in sequence.

The incident-ready gate asks: are all stages present? It refuses to publish until the paved road is complete.
Treat the platform as a product: the golden path only wins when it's more complete than any detour, so teams stop routing around it.

Verification evidence — Provisioning dry-run: `terraform plan` on the template's env step returns a clean plan; `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f service.yaml` passes admission policy. · Telemetry check: `opentelemetry collector config validate` passes and a test signal (trace + metric) reaches the backend; at least one SLO burn alert is wired. · Secrets review: no plaintext secret in the repo or manifests — every secret is a vault reference; a reviewer can confirm this by grep. · Ownership + support path: the service has a named owner in the catalog and a runbook link that resolves; the on-call knows where to look at 2 a.m. · Developer feedback loop: one product team ran the path end-to-end and did NOT hand-build any stage — if they went off-road, name which stage forced it and repair that stage.

Transfer evidence — The same reasoning moves to any constraint. In a small team, the golden path is lighter — a Makefile and a checklist can pave the road because the risk surface is small. In a regulated enterprise, the same path gains mandatory policy gates, audit trails, and change approvals, and the secrets stage becomes non-negotiable. At high scale, the path must template not one service but hundreds, so env creation and observability must be self-serve and quota-aware. What stays invariant: every stage a service crosses to go live must be paved, ownership stays explicit, and the paved road must beat the detour. What changes is how heavy each stage is. This packet — platform_golden_path_review_packet.md, with its template contract, three kill-tests, and residual-risk register — is the exact artifact your capstone reuses: not 'I understand golden paths' but 'here is a paved path I built, dry-ran, instrumented, and defended.' Carry it forward.

self-service-controls.text: A product team wants to launch a new service. They open the platform portal, click "Create Service," and forty minutes later they are in a Slack thread begging an SRE for a namespace, a secret, and a pipeline — because the portal generated a repo but not a running system. The golden path was a facade, so the team paved their own road around it.

Self-service controls are the boundary and ownership problem of platform governance: the platform must lower cognitive load enough that teams take the paved road, without hiding who owns the service or what risk it carries. This lesson produces Section 1 of the golden-path packet you defend into the capstone.

The template generates CI/CD and environment creation — the first stage that must actually work self-serve, not just scaffold a repo.

cost-and-quota-guardrails.text: The golden path shipped, adoption soared, and the platform team high-fived — until the monthly cloud bill tripled because forty teams each requested 8 CPU 'just to be safe' and nothing on the paved road ever said no. The VP's question in the review is one sentence: 'Who approved this, and where was the guardrail?'

A golden path that makes shipping frictionless also makes overspending frictionless unless the paved road itself enforces limits. Cost and quota guardrails are the layer that keeps a self-service platform from becoming a self-service blank check — and they must live at admission, not in a doc teams skip.

cost-and-quota-guardrails.prompt: Your platform's service template ships with a comment: '# Remember to set sensible resource limits.' A team copies the template, leaves the limits blank, and deploys 20 replicas at 8 CPU each. What actually went wrong here — the team, or the platform?
cost-and-quota-guardrails.reveal: The platform. 'Remember to...' is not a guardrail; it is a hope. The failure mode of every internal developer platform is exactly this: teams bypass the intended path because templates, quotas, and support are incomplete, so the easy thing and the safe thing point in different directions. A real guardrail makes the blank-limits deploy REJECTED at admission — the platform says no before the bill says it for you. The comment quietly moved a platform responsibility onto forty product teams who will each optimize for their own headroom.

cost-and-quota-guardrails.intro: The guardrail artifact, one block at a time. Trace the complete platform artifact before implementing its deterministic evidence model.
cost-and-quota-guardrails.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-orders-quota
  namespace: team-orders
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"          # namespace-wide ceiling, not per-pod
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    limits.cpu: "12"
    limits.memory: 24Gi
    pods: "40"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: team-orders-defaults
  namespace: team-orders
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:            { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }   # applied when blank
      defaultRequest:     { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
      max:                { cpu: "2",  memory: 2Gi }       # per-container ceiling
---
# Gatekeeper: every namespace on the golden path MUST carry a cost-center label
# and a ResourceQuota, or admission is denied.
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: golden-path-requires-quota
spec:
  match:
    kinds: [{ apiGroups: [""], kinds: ["Namespace"] }]
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels: { platform.sage/golden-path: "true" }
  parameters:
    requiredLabels: ["platform.sage/cost-center"]
steps: The ResourceQuota is the ceiling: This caps the WHOLE namespace, so 'each team grabs 8 CPU to be safe' can no longer sum to a blank check. requests are what you pay for reserving; limits are the burst cap.
Cap pod count too: Runaway replica counts (a bad HPA, a crash-loop scale-up) are a real cost failure. A pods ceiling bounds the blast radius of a misconfigured autoscaler.
LimitRange defaults the blank case: This is the fix for the pretest: a container with no limits does NOT get unlimited resources — it gets 250m/256Mi. The dangerous default becomes a safe default.
And ceilings each container: max stops one greedy pod from eating the whole namespace quota. Defaults protect the forgetful; max protects against the aggressive.

Gatekeeper makes it non-bypassable: The RETURN-'no' move: a golden-path namespace with no cost-center label or no quota is DENIED at admission. This is what turns 'remember to...' into a guardrail teams cannot skip.

cost-and-quota-guardrails.title: A guardrail is enforced at admission, defaulted sanely, and observable
cost-and-quota-guardrails.text: Cap spend where the platform CAN say no: a ResourceQuota bounds a namespace, a LimitRange defaults and ceilings per-pod, an OPA/admission gate rejects non-conforming manifests, and a budget alert watches the trend. Enforced, not documented — the paved road refuses the unsafe deploy.

#
# Mission: Take one namespace on your internal platform's golden path and add cost and quota guardrails: a ResourceQuota + LimitRange that caps spend, a budget alert threshold, and a policy gate that BLOCKS a service template from shipping unless it declares its quota. Write it up as a decision packet another platform engineer can inspect.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Run kubectl apply --dry-run=server against a namespace with no ResourceQuota using a blank-limits manifest. If it is ADMITTED, your guardrail is decoration — the enforcement is missing.
# 2. Confirm the LimitRange defaults a container that declares no limits (describe the pod: it should carry 250m/256Mi, not 'unlimited').
# 3. Check the Gatekeeper/admission constraint DENIES a golden-path namespace missing the cost-center label — capture the exact denial message.
# 4. Confirm a budget or quota-utilization alert exists with a concrete threshold (e.g. 80% of requests.cpu), not just a dashboard someone must remember to open.
# 5. Name the owner: every namespace on the path carries a cost-center label so showback can attribute spend. Unattributed cost is a guardrail with no one to page.

# Local execution is practice feedback; it does not create controlled mastery evidence.

ALERT_AT = 0.80

    ("orders-api-1",   500),
    ("orders-api-2",   500),
    ("orders-worker",  None),    # blank — LimitRange must default it
    ("batch-backfill", 4000),
    ("batch-backfill-2", 4000),  # this one crosses the ceiling
    ("cron-cleanup",   None),
]

def admit(pods, quota_m, default_m):
    # TODO: implement the platform decision from the supplied delivery fixtures.
    # Preserve failure discrimination and the exact observable contract.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the platform evidence decision")

decisions, used, utilization, alert = admit(PODS, QUOTA_CPU_M, DEFAULT_REQUEST_M)
for pod, eff, source, verdict in decisions:
    print(f"{pod}: {eff}m ({source}) -> {verdict}")
print(f"namespace_usage: {used}m / {QUOTA_CPU_M}m = {utilization:.0%}")

storyboard.say: It starts here: a service template scaffolds the deploy manifest, the frictionless entry point onto the paved road.
CI runs policy checks, then does kubectl apply, handing the manifest to the admission controller.
Admission is the moment of truth: the one place the platform can actually say no before any cost lands.
A manifest with blank limits and no quota is over cap, so admission rejects it outright.
The fix is to declare a quota: a conforming manifest passes admission and lands in the namespace.
The namespace consumes cloud resources, and billing tallies the real spend it produced.
Billing feeds a budget alert that watches cost by namespace, then loops back to tune template defaults.
The lesson: billing and alerts only observe. Enforce limits at admission, or the paved road becomes a blank check.

cost-and-quota-guardrails.title: The guardrail artifact, one block at a time
cost-and-quota-guardrails.subtitle: ResourceQuota + LimitRange + a Gatekeeper constraint that REJECTS a namespace with no quota. This is the enforced version of the template comment.
cost-and-quota-guardrails.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-orders-quota
  namespace: team-orders
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"          # namespace-wide ceiling, not per-pod
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    limits.cpu: "12"
    limits.memory: 24Gi
    pods: "40"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: team-orders-defaults
  namespace: team-orders
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:            { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }   # applied when blank
      defaultRequest:     { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
      max:                { cpu: "2",  memory: 2Gi }       # per-container ceiling
---
# Gatekeeper: every namespace on the golden path MUST carry a cost-center label
# and a ResourceQuota, or admission is denied.
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: golden-path-requires-quota
spec:
  match:
    kinds: [{ apiGroups: [""], kinds: ["Namespace"] }]
    labelSelector:
      matchLabels: { platform.sage/golden-path: "true" }
  parameters:
    requiredLabels: ["platform.sage/cost-center"]

steps.label: The ResourceQuota is the ceiling
steps.note: This caps the WHOLE namespace, so 'each team grabs 8 CPU to be safe' can no longer sum to a blank check. requests are what you pay for reserving; limits are the burst cap.

steps.label: Cap pod count too
steps.note: Runaway replica counts (a bad HPA, a crash-loop scale-up) are a real cost failure. A pods ceiling bounds the blast radius of a misconfigured autoscaler.

steps.label: LimitRange defaults the blank case
steps.note: This is the fix for the pretest: a container with no limits does NOT get unlimited resources — it gets 250m/256Mi. The dangerous default becomes a safe default.

steps.label: And ceilings each container
steps.note: max stops one greedy pod from eating the whole namespace quota. Defaults protect the forgetful; max protects against the aggressive.

steps.label: Gatekeeper makes it non-bypassable
steps.note: The RETURN-'no' move: a golden-path namespace with no cost-center label or no quota is DENIED at admission. This is what turns 'remember to...' into a guardrail teams cannot skip.

cost-and-quota-guardrails.text: The senior FinOps-on-platform move is default sane, cap hard, and always attribute. Quotas that are too tight generate a flood of exception tickets and teams route around the platform — the exact bypass failure you were trying to prevent. Set defaults from real p95 usage (showback data tells you), make the hard cap generous enough that normal work never hits it, and require a cost-center label so every dollar has an owner. A guardrail nobody can live inside is just a slower way to lose adoption.

cost-and-quota-guardrails.question: A reviewer challenges your guardrail: 'You showed me a ResourceQuota YAML. How do I know it is actually PROVEN and not just described?' Which response is the real proof?
options: Point to the template README section that documents the recommended CPU limits.
Show the kubectl apply --dry-run=server output where a blank-limits, quota-less deploy is REJECTED by admission, plus a budget-alert screenshot at the 80% threshold.
Explain that the team has agreed in standup to always set limits going forward.
Show that the ResourceQuota object exists in the cluster via kubectl get resourcequota.
cost-and-quota-guardrails.explanation: Proof is a guardrail biting. Option 4 shows the quota EXISTS but not that it ENFORCES — a quota with no LimitRange still admits blank-limit pods against it, and an object can exist while being unmatched. Options 1 and 3 are documented intent, which is precisely the bypassable failure mode. Only option 2 replays the failure (a non-conforming deploy) and shows it rejected, then shows the trend watcher firing — executable + observable, exactly the two-layer proof the lesson demands.

cost-and-quota-guardrails.excellent: Passing evidence plus a new failure fixture, retained regression, explicit rejected option, and this transfer: The same move — put the limit where the system can say no, default it sanely, attribute every unit — travels across every scale. On a small team, a single ResourceQuota per namespace and a Slack budget alert is enough; the ceremony would only slow you down. In a regulated enterprise, the guardrail becomes a Terraform-enforced quota module with an OPA policy library, an approval workflow for exceptions, and chargeback (real cross-team billing) instead of showback. At high scale, you add per-tenant quotas, autoscaler caps, and anomaly detection on the spend trend so a single misconfigured HPA cannot run for a weekend. What stays invariant everywhere: enforcement lives on the paved road, not in a doc — and the proof is always a deploy the platform refused. Carry your decision packet forward; the capstone reuses this exact guardrail as the cost layer of the golden-path review packet, so a platform that is easy to adopt is also impossible to overspend on.

support-model.outcome: Design the support model for a golden path a product team must adopt to launch a new service — the tiers, ownership boundaries, escalation, and SLOs — and write it as a reviewable packet that proves teams will not bypass the platform.
support-model.proof: platform_golden_path_review_packet.md with a support-tier table (L0 self-serve → L3 platform on-call), an ownership boundary (what the platform owns vs. what the team owns), an escalation path with response SLOs, one named inspection-hook output, and a paired platform_golden_path_risk_register.md naming the top three risks that survive the decision.
support-model.unlock: Your packet names the tiers, draws the platform/team ownership line, attaches one hook output (terraform plan | kubectl --dry-run | helm template), and states what would make teams bypass the path.
support-model.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a support model if it is only an on-call rotation. A rotation answers 'who gets paged'; a support model answers 'at which tier does each request resolve, who owns it, and what happens when the golden path does not cover the case.' A rotation without tiers or an ownership boundary is a phone number, not a model.

support-model.text: The platform team ships a beautiful Backstage portal with a one-click service template — and three weeks later half the product teams are copy-pasting last year's Helm chart in a side channel because the template had no secrets story and nobody knew who to ask when it broke. The portal was real; the support model was missing, so the golden path became the abandoned path.

This lesson sits in Platform Governance And Scale: a golden path only counts as adopted if teams trust that when it breaks, someone owns the repair. The support model is the operational contract underneath the template — the Section that turns a self-serve portal into a path teams actually stay on.

support-model.prompt: Your golden path has a slick service template and a clean terraform plan. Adoption is still stalling. Before reading on — what operational thing is almost certainly missing?
support-model.reveal: A support model with a defended ownership boundary. Teams do not bypass a portal because the UI is ugly; they bypass it because when the template fails at 4 p.m. — a secret won't mount, an environment won't provision — there is no named tier that owns the fix and no SLO on the response. 'Beautiful template, unclear who to page' is the exact shape of a golden path that quietly dies. Adoption is a trust artifact, not a UX artifact.

support-model.intro: Writing the support model, one section at a time. Trace the complete platform artifact before implementing its deterministic evidence model.
support-model.code:
## Support Model — checkout-service golden path
| Tier | Owner | Channel | Response SLO | Resolves |
| L0 | (self) | portal docs + runbook | instant | template usage, env matrix |
| L1 | (self) | Backstage service template | instant | scaffold + CI/CD + namespace |
| L2 | platform (office hours) | #platform-help | 4h | provisioning + secrets failures |
| L3 | platform on-call | PagerDuty | 30m | golden-path outage / blocked launch |

- Ownership boundary: platform owns the TEMPLATE, provisioning, secrets wiring,
  and observability defaults; the team owns SERVICE CODE, its SLOs, and business config.
- Escalation trigger: any L1 failure a team cannot self-resolve in 15 min -> L2.
- Bypass tripwire: >2 side-channel deploys/week means the path is not trusted -> audit.

# Inspection hook (proof the path provisions before we promise support on it):
$ terraform plan -out=checkout.plan
Plan: 7 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
$ kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f service.yaml
service/checkout configured (server dry run)
steps: The tier table: Four tiers, each with an OWNER and a response SLO. 'Owner: (self)' at L0/L1 is the point — self-serve is a tier, not the absence of support. Without the SLO column this is a wiki page, not a contract.

Platform-owned tiers L2/L3: The 4h office-hours tier and the 30m paged tier are where trust is won or lost. A golden path with no paged tier for a blocked launch is the exact reason teams keep their old chart around.

The ownership boundary: The single most-skipped line. Platform owns template + provisioning + secrets + observability; team owns their code + business SLOs. Blur this and you get either a bottleneck or an orphaned failure.

Escalation trigger + bypass tripwire: The tripwire (>2 side-channel deploys/week) makes bypass MEASURABLE — it turns 'are teams adopting?' from a vibe into a signal you can put on an adoption scorecard.

Inspection-hook output: You cannot promise support on a path you have not proven provisions. terraform plan + kubectl --dry-run=server are the cheap disqualifiers — run them BEFORE the packet claims the path is supportable.
support-model.commonMistake: Teams keep the old chart as a lifeboat — path dies

support-model.title: A support model is tiers + an ownership boundary + escalation SLOs — not a rotation
support-model.text: Define resolution tiers (L0 docs → L1 self-serve template → L2 platform-assisted → L3 platform on-call), draw the line between what the platform owns and what the team owns, and attach a response SLO to each escalation. The invariant: every failure of the golden path resolves at a named tier with a named owner.

support-model.starter:
# Writing the support model, one section at a time
#
# Mission: Design the support model for a golden path a product team must adopt to launch a new service — the tiers, ownership boundaries, escalation, and SLOs — and write it as a reviewable packet that proves teams will not bypass the platform.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. The tier table has a named owner AND a response SLO on every row. A tier without an SLO is a suggestion, not a contract — fix it.
# 2. The ownership boundary rules out at least one failure class from each side: name one thing the platform will NOT fix (team business logic) and one the team must NOT own (secrets wiring). If the line is not defensible, it is decoration.
# 3. At least one inspection hook has real output attached (terraform plan, kubectl apply --dry-run=server, or helm template) proving the path provisions before you promise support on it.
# 4. The bypass tripwire is a concrete, countable signal (e.g. side-channel deploys/week) that lands on the adoption scorecard — not 'teams seem happy'.
# 5. The failure path folds back: name the mechanism by which an L3 repair becomes an L1 self-serve fix next time. If repairs do not improve the template, the path decays.
# 6. platform_golden_path_risk_register.md exists and names the top three risks that survive the decision (e.g. secrets rotation gap, environment drift, on-call burnout).
#
# Work only in the TODO function. Run every fixture and compare every output line.
# Local execution is practice feedback; it does not create controlled mastery evidence.

# Ownership boundary: which failure classes belong to which side
PLATFORM_OWNS = {"template", "provisioning", "secrets-wiring", "observability-defaults"}
TEAM_OWNS = {"service-code", "service-slo", "business-config"}

# Tier SLOs in minutes (first response)
TIER_SLO = {"L2": 240, "L3": 30}

TICKETS = [
    # (id, failure_class, minutes_open, self_resolve_attempted)

storyboard.say: A product team opens the Backstage portal and requests a new service through the one-click template — this is the golden path's entry point.
The portal renders the template and provisioning kicks off — secrets, env, and infrastructure are supposed to materialize automatically.
Here's the risk: provisioning may break — a secret won't mount, an env won't provision — and now the team is stuck with no obvious owner.
Instead of a side-channel copy-paste, the failure escalates to L2 platform-assisted support, within a named response SLO.
If L2 can't resolve it, they page L3 — the platform on-call — so every failure lands on a named owner, never a dead end.
On-call root-causes the break and ships a template fix — the repair is captured, not just patched for one team.
The fix flows back into the portal so the same failure self-serves next time — that feedback loop is what makes a golden path teams actually stay on.

A staff engineer opens a terminal, runs the template's own dry-run, and it fails on a missing secret binding — the path nobody actually walked. The room goes quiet, because the roadmap reviewed the slide, not the platform.

A platform roadmap review decides which golden paths ship and which get held back under release risk. Handled shallowly, the platform builds a portal teams bypass — because templates, environments, secrets, and support paths were reviewed on paper, never proven.

platform-roadmap-review.prompt: 'The golden path is on the roadmap and the Backstage template exists — mark it green.' Before you sign off, what is wrong with that as review evidence? Answer before reading on.
platform-roadmap-review.reveal: A template existing proves nothing about whether a team can walk it. 'Green' here means the slide is green, not the path. The real review runs the template's own dry-run: `kubectl apply --dry-run=server`, `terraform plan`, `helm template`, secrets check. Golden paths bypass the platform precisely at the step nobody inspected — a missing env, an unresolved secret, a support path that dead-ends. Reviewing the roadmap means proving the path, not confirming the artifact is on the board.

# Golden Path Review Packet — orders-service template
## Context
- Roadmap item: golden path for stateless HTTP services, target adoption 80% by Q3
## Constraint
- Non-negotiable: no daytime downtime on the release path; secrets never in repo
## Selected approach
- Backstage scaffolder template + Helm chart + Terraform env module
## Rejected approach
- Wiki runbook of manual steps — REJECTED: no dry-run, drifts under release risk
## Verification (inspection hooks, output attached)
- kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f rendered.yaml  -> server dry run: PASS
- terraform plan -> Plan: 6 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy
- helm template . | grep -c secretKeyRef -> 2 (bound via ExternalSecret, none inline)
## Expected failure
- Missing secret binding: template renders, dry-run passes, deploy fails at runtime
## Reviewer objection
- "Is this proven or merely described?" -> replay the dry-run + secrets grep above
## Transfer note
- Regulated env: add OPA policy gate + change-approval before the adopt step
steps: Context: the roadmap item: Name the exact golden path and its adoption target. 'Improve DX' is a slogan; 'golden path for stateless HTTP services, 80% by Q3' is reviewable.
The operating constraint FIRST: Name the non-negotiable before the solution: no daytime downtime, no secrets in repo. A constraint that rules out at least one option — here, the manual runbook.
Selected vs rejected: The rejected option and WHY it fails under release risk is the senior move. 'Wiki runbook, rejected: no dry-run, drifts' is a decision; silence is a guess.
Two inspection hooks, output pasted: server dry-run PASS + terraform plan + helm template secrets grep. This is the line that separates proven from described — a reviewer can replay it.
The expected failure: The realistic one: template renders and dry-run passes, but the secret binding is missing so runtime deploy fails. Name it before it names you.
Reviewer objection + repair: 'Proven or merely described?' answered by the replayable hooks above. That closes the loop the roadmap review exists to close.
Transfer note: Change the environment, not the wording: a regulated env adds an OPA policy gate + change approval before adoption. Same reasoning, stricter bar.

# Writing the review packet, one line at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real golden-path decision your platform faces (or a realistic one) and write platform_golden_path_review_packet.md: the operating constraint, the selected approach, the rejected approach, the expected failure, the verification method with inspection-hook output, one reviewer objection, and a transfer note.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. The operating constraint is stated BEFORE the selected approach, and it rules out at least one plausible option (the rejected one).
# 2. At least two inspection hooks ran and their output is pasted: kubectl apply --dry-run=server, terraform plan, helm template, or otel collector validate.
# 3. The rejected approach is recorded with why it fails under release or review risk — not just which one you picked.
# 4. The expected failure is realistic and specific (e.g. missing secret binding fails at runtime), not 'something breaks'.
# 5. The invalidation condition is written: the exact result where the golden path looks acceptable in review but fails when release risk changes.
# 6. The transfer note changes the environment (regulated / high-scale / small team), not just the wording.
#
# Work only in the TODO function. Run every fixture and compare every output line.
# Local execution is practice feedback; it does not create controlled mastery evidence.

ROADMAP = [
    {
        "item": "golden-path: stateless http services",
        "claimed": "green",
        "proofs": [
            ("decision",    "constraint + rejected option recorded",        True),
            ("operational", "kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f rendered",   True),
            ("operational", "terraform plan: 6 add / 0 destroy",            True),
            ("operational", "grep secret-name env for inline value: -> empty = none inline", True),
            ("transfer",    "regulated-env note: adds OPA gate",            True),
        ],
    },
    {
        "item": "golden-path: batch/cron services",
        "claimed": "green",
        "proofs": [
            ("decision",    "described in the roadmap deck",                False),
            ("operational", "template exists in Backstage",                 False),
        ],
    },
    {
        "item": "secrets: externalize to vault",
        "claimed": "green",
        "proofs": [
            ("decision",    "constraint + rejected option recorded",        True),
            ("operational", "template dry-run FAILED: missing secret binding", False),
        ],
    },
]

REQUIRED_KINDS = ("decision", "operational", "transfer")

def review(items):
    # TODO: implement the platform decision from the supplied delivery fixtures.
    # Preserve failure discrimination and the exact observable contract.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the platform evidence decision")

verdicts = review(ROADMAP)
honest_green = 0
inflated = 0
for item, claimed, green, missing, failed in verdicts:
    actual = "green" if green else "NOT green"
    if green:
        honest_green += 1
        print(f"{item}: {actual}")
    else:
        inflated += 1 if claimed == "green" else 0
        why = f"missing proof: {', '.join(missing)}" if missing else "hooks failed"
        print(f"{item}: {actual} (claimed {claimed}) — {why}")
        for d in failed:
            print(f"  failed/absent: {d}")

storyboard.say: Every roadmap item starts here, and the golden path only earns adoption by generating a real service template.
The template can't be trusted on a slide — it must actually dry-run through CI/CD before anything else.
Only on a passing dry-run does the plan advance to the infrastructure-as-code gate.
And only when the IaC plan passes does the item reach the secrets and telemetry check — the one that usually breaks.
When the dry-run, IaC plan, and secrets check are all green, the path is proven and can be marked adopted.
But a missing secret binding sends it down the bypass path — the failure the roadmap slide never showed.
Bypass isn't the end: the item loops back to repair and re-review, because green means proven, not described.

# Golden Path Review Packet — orders-service template
## Context
- Roadmap item: golden path for stateless HTTP services, target adoption 80% by Q3
## Constraint
- Non-negotiable: no daytime downtime on the release path; secrets never in repo
## Selected approach
- Backstage scaffolder template + Helm chart + Terraform env module
## Rejected approach
- Wiki runbook of manual steps — REJECTED: no dry-run, drifts under release risk
## Verification (inspection hooks, output attached)
- kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f rendered.yaml  -> server dry run: PASS
- terraform plan -> Plan: 6 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy
- helm template . | grep -c secretKeyRef -> 2 (bound via ExternalSecret, none inline)
## Expected failure
- Missing secret binding: template renders, dry-run passes, deploy fails at runtime
## Reviewer objection
- "Is this proven or merely described?" -> replay the dry-run + secrets grep above
## Transfer note
- Regulated env: add OPA policy gate + change-approval before the adopt step

steps.label: Context: the roadmap item
steps.note: Name the exact golden path and its adoption target. 'Improve DX' is a slogan; 'golden path for stateless HTTP services, 80% by Q3' is reviewable.

steps.label: The operating constraint FIRST
steps.note: Name the non-negotiable before the solution: no daytime downtime, no secrets in repo. A constraint that rules out at least one option — here, the manual runbook.

steps.label: Selected vs rejected
steps.note: The rejected option and WHY it fails under release risk is the senior move. 'Wiki runbook, rejected: no dry-run, drifts' is a decision; silence is a guess.

steps.label: Two inspection hooks, output pasted
steps.note: server dry-run PASS + terraform plan + helm template secrets grep. This is the line that separates proven from described — a reviewer can replay it.

steps.label: The expected failure
steps.note: The realistic one: template renders and dry-run passes, but the secret binding is missing so runtime deploy fails. Name it before it names you.

steps.label: Reviewer objection + repair
steps.note: 'Proven or merely described?' answered by the replayable hooks above. That closes the loop the roadmap review exists to close.

steps.label: Transfer note
steps.note: Change the environment, not the wording: a regulated env adds an OPA policy gate + change approval before adoption. Same reasoning, stricter bar.
